question: In each cell of a $4 \times 4$ grid, one of the two diagonals is drawn uniformly at random. Compute the probability that the resulting $32$ triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors.

completions.text:
We will show that if each cell of a 4×4 grid is independently given one of the two possible diagonals (each with probability ½), then the 32 resulting triangular regions can be 2‐colored (red and blue, with adjacent regions getting different colors) if and only if a certain “column–relation” condition holds. In the end one may prove that exactly 128 out of the 2^16 = 65,536 possible diagonal–assignments yield a bipartite “region–graph” (one in which every edge joins regions of opposite colors), so the desired probability is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A. Setting Up the Problem

1. In each of the 16 cells a diagonal is drawn. (There are 2^16 equally likely outcomes.) Each cell is a unit square with vertices (say) top‐left, top–right, bottom–right, and bottom–left. The two possible diagonals are:
  • “/” (from top–right to bottom–left)
  • “\” (from top–left to bottom–right)

2. The diagonal splits the cell into 2 triangles. (Thus there are 32 triangles overall.) Note that the two triangles in a cell share the diagonal (an edge in the region–graph) and so must receive opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring.

3. However, triangles in different cells can also share a full side (an edge that is part of the boundary between two cells). (The outer boundary of the grid does not “cause trouble” since it is not shared.) Thus the only potential “cross–cell” conflicts occur along the grid lines separating adjacent cells.

──────────────────────────────
B. A Useful Way to Think About the Coloring

Because each cell’s two triangles must receive opposite colors, one may “fix a convention” in each cell. For example, in every cell declare that the triangle that touches the top edge is colored red and the other (bottom) triangle blue. (Of course, one is free to swap the colors in a given cell; this freedom is equivalent to having a “local sign” in each cell.)

Now label the cells by coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i, j ≤ 4. In cell (i, j) let x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 0 if we choose the convention so that the top–edge triangle is red and 1 if we choose the opposite. (Thus the cell’s two triangles get colors red and blue in a fixed way once x₍ᵢⱼ₎ is chosen.)

Next, note that the only “cross–cell” adjacencies occur along the common boundaries. There are two types:

• Vertical neighbors (cells in the same column, one directly above the other).  
 – The bottom triangle of the upper cell (which is the “opposite” of the top triangle) meets the top triangle of the lower cell.  
 – Since the bottom triangle’s color is the opposite of x₍ᵢⱼ₎ and the top triangle’s color is x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎, the condition for these two triangles to have opposite colors is  
  not x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 1 – x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎  or equivalently  x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎.

• Horizontal neighbors (cells in the same row, one immediately to the right of the other).  
 – In a given cell the triangle touching the right edge depends on the diagonal:
  ○ In a “/” cell the right–edge triangle is the bottom one (its color is not x₍ᵢⱼ₎).
  ○ In a “\” cell the right–edge triangle is the top one (its color is x₍ᵢⱼ₎).
 – Similarly, in the cell to the right the triangle touching the left edge is:
  ○ In a “/” cell the left–edge triangle is the top one (color x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
  ○ In a “\” cell the left–edge triangle is the bottom one (color not x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).

Thus, for a horizontal edge shared by cell (i, j) on the left and cell (i, j+1) on the right the condition is:
  if cell (i,j) is “/” and cell (i,j+1) is “/”, then
   not x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 1 – x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎  ⟹ x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.
  if cell (i,j) is “/” and cell (i,j+1) is “\”, then
   not x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 1 – (not x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎)  ⟹ x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = not x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.
  if cell (i,j) is “\” and cell (i,j+1) is “/”, then
   x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 1 – x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎  ⟹ x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = not x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.
  if cell (i,j) is “\” and cell (i,j+1) is “\”, then
   x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = 1 – (not x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎)  ⟹ x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.

In summary, for a horizontal edge the rule is:
  – If the two adjacent cells have the same diagonal orientation, then x₍ᵢⱼ₎ must equal x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.
  – If they have opposite orientations, then x₍ᵢⱼ₎ must be the opposite of x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.

But recall that the vertical condition forced all cells in a given column to have the same x–value. (For if x₍ᵢⱼ₎ = x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ for every i, then we may define yⱼ to be the common value in column j.) Thus, if we denote by yⱼ the common “color–choice” in column j (which comes from every cell in that column), then the horizontal condition becomes, for every row i and for each adjacent pair of columns j and j+1:
  – If the diagonal in cell (i, j) and the diagonal in cell (i, j+1) are the same, then yⱼ = y₍ⱼ₊₁₎.
  – If they are different, then yⱼ = not y₍ⱼ₊₁₎.

Now here is the key point: The number yⱼ is independent of i. Therefore, for a fixed pair of adjacent columns j and j+1 the condition “must hold for every row i”. In other words, for each j = 1, 2, 3 the relation between the diagonals in column j and column j+1 (when read row–by–row) must be the same in every row. That is, for each adjacent column pair either
  (a) in every row the cell in column j and the cell in column j+1 have the same diagonal, or
  (b) in every row they have opposite diagonals.

──────────────────────────────
C. Counting the “Good” Configurations

Now, think of the grid column–by–column. In column j the 4 cells give a 4–bit vector (each bit being 0 for “/” and 1 for “\”). Call this vector vⱼ. The condition we derived is that for each adjacent pair of columns j and j+1 the 4–bit vectors must be either equal or opposites. In other words, for j = 1, 2, 3 we must have

  v₍ⱼ₊₁₎ = vⱼ  or  v₍ⱼ₊₁₎ = not vⱼ.

How many choices are there?
  • v₁ can be any of 2⁴ = 16 vectors.
  • Then v₂ is forced to be either v₁ or its complement (2 choices).
  • Then v₃ is either v₂ or its complement (2 choices).
  • Then v₄ is either v₃ or its complement (2 choices).

Thus the total number of “good” assignments is 16 × 2³ = 16 × 8 = 128.

Since the total number of assignments is 2^(16) = 65,536, the probability that a random drawing yields a configuration whose 32 regions can be 2–colored is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
D. Final Answer

The answer to the problem is 1/512.

So, the probability that the 32 triangular regions (formed by drawing one of the two diagonals in each cell of a 4×4 grid) can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is 1/512.

We start with a 4×4 grid of squares. In each square (cell) one of the two possible diagonals is drawn at random (each with probability ½), and this diagonal splits the square into 2 triangular regions. (Thus there are 16 cells and 32 triangles in all.) We wish to know the probability that the 32 regions can be colored red and blue in such a way that any two regions which share an entire edge (that is, a common boundary segment, not just a point) receive different colors.

A useful way to attack the problem is to “encode” the situation by keeping track, in each cell, of which of the two triangles touches which part of the cell’s boundary. (Remember that although the diagonal inside a cell is an edge between the two triangles in that cell, it is not shared with any triangle in an adjacent cell.) Once we understand which triangles in neighboring cells might “meet” along a grid edge, we can translate the coloring condition into a set of equations.

Step 1. Labeling the Triangles in a Cell

Label the vertices of a typical square cell as follows:
  • Top‐left: TL
  • Top‐right: TR
  • Bottom‐right: BR
  • Bottom‐left: BL

There are two choices for the diagonal:
1. If the diagonal is drawn from TL to BR (we’ll call this “type A” or “/”), then the cell is divided into:
  – Triangle T₁ with vertices TL, TR, BR (this triangle touches the top and right edges).
  – Triangle T₂ with vertices TL, BR, BL (this triangle touches the left and bottom edges).

2. If the diagonal is drawn from TR to BL (we’ll call this “type B” or “\”), then the cell is divided into:
  – Triangle T₁ with vertices TL, TR, BL (this triangle touches the top and left edges).
  – Triangle T₂ with vertices TR, BR, BL (this triangle touches the right and bottom edges).

In every cell the two triangles share the drawn diagonal. Since they share an edge, they must receive opposite colors in any proper 2‐coloring. (That is, if we “declare” one triangle to be, say, red then the other must be blue.)

Step 2. How Triangles in Adjacent Cells Meet

The only edges that are shared between triangles in different cells are segments along the grid lines (the boundaries between cells). There are two types of such shared edges: vertical edges (between horizontally adjacent cells) and horizontal edges (between vertically adjacent cells).

• Vertical edges (between a cell in column j and the one in column j+1):

 – In the left cell:
  • If the cell is type A, the triangle touching the right edge is T₁.
  • If the cell is type B, the triangle touching the right edge is T₂.
 – In the right cell:
  • If that cell is type A, the triangle touching the left edge is T₂.
  • If that cell is type B, the triangle touching the left edge is T₁.

Thus, when two horizontally adjacent cells share a vertical edge, the “color” coming from the left cell depends on its type and the “color” coming from the right cell depends on its type. (Remember: in any cell the two triangles are oppositely colored. So if we “declare” a color for T₁ in a cell then T₂ automatically gets the opposite color.)

• Horizontal edges (between a cell in row i and the one in row i+1):

 – In the upper cell, the triangle touching the bottom edge is always T₂ (regardless of type).
 – In the lower cell, the triangle touching the top edge is always T₁ (regardless of type).

Thus, along a horizontal edge the color coming from the upper cell is the opposite of the “base color” we assign to that row (since T₂ is opposite to T₁), while the lower cell contributes its T₁ color.

Step 3. Encoding the Coloring by “Row Variables”

Because the only “free” choice we have is how to assign the colors in each cell subject to the rule that the two triangles in one cell are opposites, we can do the following. In each cell, choose an arbitrary “base color” for triangle T₁ and let T₂ get the opposite color. (It does not matter which triangle we call T₁; the key point is that once the diagonal is drawn the two triangles must get opposite colors.)

Now, let X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ be the color (say, 0 for red and 1 for blue) assigned to T₁ in the cell in row i and column j. Then the triangle that touches a boundary will have a color that is either X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ or its opposite, depending on the cell’s type and which edge is involved.

Examine the shared edges:

A. Horizontal edges (between row i and row i+1):
 – The bottom edge of the cell in row i is always part of T₂, so its color is 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎.
 – The top edge of the cell in row i+1 is always part of T₁, so its color is X₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎.
For the two regions meeting along this edge to have opposite colors we need:
  1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ ≠ X₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎.
But since 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ is exactly the opposite of X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎, the only way this inequality can hold is if
  X₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎.
In other words, every two cells in consecutive rows (in the same column) must have the same base color.

B. Vertical edges (between column j and column j+1):
 – In the left cell (column j):
  • If the cell is type A, the triangle along the right edge is T₁ (color X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎).
  • If the cell is type B, the triangle along the right edge is T₂ (color 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎).
 – In the right cell (column j+1):
  • If that cell is type A, the triangle along the left edge is T₂ (color 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
  • If that cell is type B, the triangle along the left edge is T₁ (color X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
For the two regions meeting along this vertical edge to have opposite colors we need:
  (if left cell is A and right cell is A) X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = 1 – (1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎) = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎,
  (if left cell is A and right cell is B) X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎,
  (if left cell is B and right cell is A) (1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎) = 1 – (1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎) = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎  (which again gives X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎),
  (if left cell is B and right cell is B) (1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎) = 1 – X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎  (which gives X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
Thus, for vertical neighbors the condition is:
  • If the two adjacent cells have the same type (both A or both B), then X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ must equal X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.
  • If they have opposite types, then X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ must be the opposite of X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎.

Step 4. Deducing the “Global” Constraints

Notice that the horizontal condition forces every cell in a given row to have the same base color. (For any fixed row i, if you look at two cells in that row sharing a horizontal edge, you must have X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ for all j.) Thus, we can think of each row as having a single “row variable” rᵢ (which is just X₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ for any j in that row).

Now, consider two vertically adjacent rows, say row i and row i+1. Look at any column j. The vertical edge between the cell in row i and the cell in row i+1 forces a relation between rᵢ and rᵢ₊₁ that depends on the types of the two cells in that column. However, since rᵢ and rᵢ₊₁ are the same for every column in their respective rows, the relation along the common edge in column j must be the same for every j. In other words, for each pair of adjacent rows the following must hold:
  Either for every column j the two cells have the same type (both A or both B) – in which case the vertical condition gives rᵢ = rᵢ₊₁,
  or for every column j the two cells have opposite types (one A and one B) – in which case the vertical condition gives rᵢ = 1 – rᵢ₊₁.
There is no “mixing” allowed: the relation between row i and row i+1 must be uniform across all 4 columns.

Step 5. Counting the “Good” Configurations

A configuration of diagonals is determined by choosing, for each of the 16 cells, whether it is type A or type B. (There are 2^16 total configurations.)

For a configuration to allow a red–blue coloring of the 32 triangles (i.e. for the graph to be bipartite), the following must hold:
  1. Each row must be “uniform” in the sense that all 4 cells in that row have the same type? Not quite – the horizontal condition only forces the base color in a row to be constant, but the row itself can be arbitrary. What is forced is the following for each pair of adjacent rows:
   • Either every cell in row i and every cell in row i+1 are of the same type,
   • Or every cell in row i and every cell in row i+1 are of opposite types.

Let’s count how many configurations satisfy this.

• First, choose the types for row 1 arbitrarily. There are 2^4 = 16 possibilities.
• Now, for row 2, the condition with row 1 must be uniform. That is, either row 2 is exactly the same as row 1 or row 2 is the complement of row 1. There are 2 choices.
• Similarly, for row 3 relative to row 2 there are 2 choices, and for row 4 relative to row 3 there are 2 choices.

Thus the number of “good” configurations is:
  16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 8 = 128.

Since the total number of configurations is 2^16 = 65,536, the desired probability is:
  128 / 65,536 = 1/512.

Step 6. Conclusion

The probability that the 32 triangular regions (formed by drawing a random diagonal in each cell of a 4×4 grid) can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge receive different colors is 1/512.

Thus, the final answer is 1/512.

    r(i) = c(j).
  • If the cell’s diagonal is “/” (recorded by a 1) then these two triangles get opposite colors so we must have
    r(i) ≠ c(j).

It is convenient to work in GF(2) (that is, with 0 and 1 where 1+1 = 0). In that language the condition “r(i) = c(j)” becomes
  r(i) + c(j) = 0  (mod 2),
and “r(i) ≠ c(j)” becomes
  r(i) + c(j) = 1  (mod 2).

Thus, if we let d(i,j) be the number (0 or 1) recording the diagonal in cell (i,j), then a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of a valid 2–coloring is that there exist numbers r(1),…,r(4) and c(1),…,c(4) in GF(2) satisfying
  r(i) + c(j) = d(i,j)  (mod 2)
for every cell (i,j).

──────────────────────────────
A little linear–algebra

There are 16 equations (one per cell) in 8 unknowns. However, it turns out that these 16 equations are “over–determined” in a very nice way. In fact one may show that a solution exists if and only if every 2×2 block (that is, every 4–cycle in the “grid–graph” on the cells) satisfies
  d(i,j) + d(i,j+1) + d(i+1,j) + d(i+1,j+1) = 0  (mod 2).
One may prove that the general solution of these 9 (not independent) equations is that the 4×4 matrix (d(i,j)) must have the “separable” form
  d(i,j) = r(i) + c(j)
for some choices of r(1),…,r(4) and c(1),…,c(4) in GF(2).

How many such matrices are there? There are 2^4 choices for the row–values r(1),…,r(4) and 2^4 choices for the column–values c(1),…,c(4). (In fact every such choice produces a matrix satisfying the 2×2 condition.) However, note that if you add a constant k to every r(i) and subtract k from every c(j) the matrix does not change. (Indeed, (r(i)+k)+(c(j)–k) = r(i)+c(j).) Thus the total number of distinct matrices is
  2^(4+4–1) = 2^7 = 128.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Since there are 2^16 = 65536 possible ways to choose the diagonals in the 16 cells and exactly 128 of these yield a matrix d(i,j) of the separable form (and hence a valid 2–coloring of the 32 regions), the desired probability is

  128/65536 = 1/512.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is 1/512.

We will show that if each cell’s diagonal is chosen at random (with two possibilities per cell, independently), then the 32 regions (triangles) can be 2‐colored (red/blue with adjacent regions opposite in color) if and only if the 16 “cell‐choices” satisfy a certain parity condition. In fact, one may prove that a valid 2–coloring exists precisely when, for every pair of adjacent columns, the “sum” (mod 2) of the diagonal–choices in that pair is the same in every row. (A similar statement holds for horizontal adjacencies, but as you will see the horizontal conditions automatically “force” the vertical ones to be consistent.) A short counting argument then shows that exactly 2^(7) out of the 2^(16) possible choices yield a bipartite (2–colorable) picture. Hence the desired probability is

  2⁷⁄2¹⁶ = 1⁄2⁹ = 1⁄512.

Below is one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Labeling the Cells and Their Diagonals

Label the 4×4 grid by rows r = 1,…,4 and columns c = 1,…,4. In each cell (r, c) one of two diagonals is drawn. (For concreteness, say that “diagonal 0” is drawn from the top–left corner to the bottom–right corner and “diagonal 1” is drawn from the top–right corner to the bottom–left corner.) Thus there are 2^(16) equally likely overall configurations.

In each cell the diagonal splits the cell into two triangles. (For example, if the cell’s corners are
  top–left: (r, c), top–right: (r, c+1), bottom–left: (r+1, c), bottom–right: (r+1, c+1),
then with diagonal 0 the two triangles are
  Triangle A: (r, c), (r, c+1), (r+1, c+1) and Triangle B: (r, c), (r+1, c), (r+1, c+1).)
Notice that in every cell the two triangles share the diagonal edge so they must receive opposite colors in any valid 2–coloring.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Setting Up a “Potential” on the Triangles

For each cell (r, c) choose a binary variable x₍r,c₎ ∈ {0,1} to represent the color of “triangle A” (say, 0 = red, 1 = blue). Then the other triangle in that cell (call it “triangle B”) gets color 1 – x₍r,c₎.

Now, when two cells share a common edge the colors on the two touching triangles must be opposite. One may check (by a short case–analysis using the picture above) that the condition for a common edge depends on the type of diagonal in the adjoining cells. (For example, if two horizontally adjacent cells share a vertical edge then one finds that if both cells have the same diagonal type the corresponding x–values must be equal, while if the cells’ diagonals differ the x–values must be opposite. In contrast, for a horizontal common edge (the bottom edge of the top cell and the top edge of the bottom cell) one always finds that the condition is x (top cell) + x (bottom cell) = 1 mod 2.)

One may show that after a little work the entire system of “edge–conditions” is equivalent to the following: For every vertical pair of adjacent columns (that is, for each c = 1, 2, 3) the “sums”
  d₍1,c₎ + d₍1,c+1₎, d₍2,c₎ + d₍2,c+1₎, d₍3,c₎ + d₍3,c+1₎, d₍4,c₎ + d₍4,c+1₎
(all computed mod 2) must all be equal. (Here d₍r,c₎ is 0 or 1 according as cell (r, c) has diagonal 0 or 1.) In other words, for each c = 1, 2, 3 there is a bit E(c) (which can be 0 or 1) so that for every row r
  d₍r,c₎ + d₍r,c+1₎ = E(c).

One may show by a “recurrence‐argument” (or by a simple counting argument) that the total number of 4×4 {0,1}–matrices d₍r,c₎ satisfying
  for each c = 1,2,3, d₍1,c₎+d₍1,c+1₎ = d₍2,c₎+d₍2,c+1₎ = d₍3,c₎+d₍3,c+1₎ = d₍4,c₎+d₍4,c+1₎
is exactly 2^(4+4–1) = 2⁷ = 128.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Concluding the Probability

Since there are 2^(16) = 65,536 total diagonal configurations and exactly 128 of these lead to a system of edge–conditions that is consistent (so that a red/blue coloring exists), the desired probability is

  128⁄65,536 = 1⁄512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be 2–colored (red and blue with adjacent regions opposite in color) is 1⁄512.

We will show that if one places, independently and uniformly at random, one of the two possible diagonals in each of the 16 unit‐squares of a 4×4 grid, then the 32 resulting triangles (each square is cut into 2 triangles by its diagonal) can be “two–colored” (red/blue so that adjacent regions get opposite colors) if and only if the “vertical” boundaries between rows have a very special property. In fact, one may prove that a valid 2–coloring exists exactly when for each horizontal “band” between two consecutive rows the 4 pairs of diagonals in the corresponding cells are “homogeneous” – that is, either in every column the two diagonals are the same or in every column they are different. (One may show that no other “cycle–obstruction” can occur.) We will explain one way to arrive at this answer and then count the number of “good” configurations.

Let us describe one way to “encode” the picture.

Step 1. Label the rows 1,…,4 and the columns 1,…,4. In each cell (i,j) choose a diagonal. (We use 0 and 1 to denote the two choices.) For later use it is convenient to “mark” each cell by a “base–color” (which you may think of as a free parameter that will later be used to “propagate” a 2–coloring of the triangles). In any given cell the two triangles must get opposite colors. (That is forced by the fact that the diagonal divides the square into two regions that share an edge.) However, the way the triangles in one cell touch triangles in a neighboring cell depends on which diagonal is drawn.

A short analysis shows that if we declare that in a given cell the “base–color” is f (which may be thought of as 0 or 1) and we write the diagonal as follows:

• If the diagonal is drawn from the top–left to the bottom–right (we call this “/”), then
  – the triangle touching the top edge gets color f,
  – the triangle touching the bottom edge gets the opposite color (not f),
  – the triangle touching the left edge gets not f, and
  – the triangle touching the right edge gets f.

• If instead the diagonal is drawn from the top–right to the bottom–left (“\”), then
  – the triangle touching the top edge gets not f,
  – the triangle touching the bottom edge gets f,
  – the triangle touching the left edge gets not f, and
  – the triangle touching the right edge gets f.

Now note that when two cells share a vertical edge (i.e. they are in the same row, with one to the left of the other) the two triangles that meet along that edge come from the “right edge” of the left cell and the “left edge” of the right cell. In either case the rule above shows that these two triangles get the colors f (from the left cell) and not f (from the right cell) if the left cell’s base–color is f. (In other words, once you insist that every cell’s two triangles get opposite colors, it turns out that in any fixed row all cells must “agree” on their base–color in order for the vertical edges inside the row to have opposite colors.) Thus one may “choose” a base–color for each row (2 choices per row, so 2^4 total choices) and then the only non–trivial conditions come from the edges between rows.

Step 2. Look at a vertical edge between two cells in consecutive rows. Suppose the cell in row i and column j has diagonal d (0 or 1) with base–color X and the cell immediately below it in row i+1 (same column j) has diagonal e with base–color Y. A short check shows that the triangle in the upper cell that touches the common edge gets
  • color X if d = 0, and
  • color not X if d = 1,
and the triangle in the lower cell that touches that edge gets
  • color Y if e = 0, and
  • color not Y if e = 1.
Since adjacent regions must get opposite colors the “vertical condition” along that edge is that
  if d = e then X and Y must be equal, and
  if d ≠ e then X and Y must be different.
Now, here is the key point. In any fixed row the base–color is the same for every cell. Thus, when you look at the entire common boundary between two consecutive rows (which consists of 4 vertical edges – one for each column) the condition for a valid 2–coloring is that either
  (a) in every column the pair (d in the upper cell, d in the lower cell) is the same (so that X = Y is required in every column), or
  (b) in every column the pair is different (so that X ≠ Y is required in every column).
In other words, for the vertical boundaries between rows i and i+1 the “pattern” of diagonals (when read column–by–column) must be homogeneous – it can’t be “mixed” (for example, sometimes equal and sometimes different).

Step 3. Counting the “good” configurations.
A configuration (that is, an assignment of a diagonal in each cell) is “good” (i.e. yields a bipartite region–graph that can be 2–colored) if and only if for each horizontal boundary (there are 3 such boundaries in a 4×4 grid, namely between rows 1–2, 2–3, and 3–4) the 4 pairs of diagonals (one from each column) are homogeneous – that is, either all 4 pairs are “equal” or all 4 are “different.”

Now, note that the rows of the grid are chosen independently. (There are 2^4 = 16 possible “strings” of 0’s and 1’s for a given row.) For a fixed horizontal boundary between, say, row i and row i+1 the following is true. In each column the pair (d in row i, d in row i+1) is an independent random pair with four possibilities, each occurring with probability 1/4. In particular, the probability that in a given column the two entries are equal is 1/2 and that they are different is also 1/2. For the entire boundary (all 4 columns) to be homogeneous we must have either
  • all 4 columns have equal entries – which happens with probability (1/2)^4 = 1/16, or
  • all 4 columns have different entries – also with probability 1/16.
Thus the probability that one horizontal boundary is homogeneous is 1/16 + 1/16 = 1/8.

Since the rows are chosen independently the number of “good” configurations is easiest counted by first choosing the first row arbitrarily (16 choices), and then for each of the 3 horizontal boundaries the next row is forced to be either exactly the same as the row above or its complement – 2 choices for each boundary. Hence the total number of good configurations is
  16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 8 = 128.
Since the total number of diagonal configurations is 2^(16) = 65,536, the desired probability is
  128/65,536 = 1/512.

Final Answer:
The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be two–colored so that adjacent regions get different colors is 1/512.

We will show that if you choose, independently and uniformly at random, one of the two possible diagonals in each of the 16 unit‐squares of a 4×4 grid, then the 32 resulting triangular regions can be “two–colored” (red/blue so that neighboring regions get different colors) if and only if a certain “global” condition is met – and a short counting argument shows that the probability of this happening is 

  1⁄512.

In what follows we describe one way to “model” the situation and count the good outcomes.

──────────────────────────────
An Outline of One Solution

(1) Setting Up the Problem

Label the 16 unit–squares by their row and column indices (i,j) with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ 4. In each square you draw one diagonal. (For concreteness, you may think of the two choices as “X–diagonal” (from the top–left to the bottom–right) and “Y–diagonal” (from the top–right to the bottom–left).) Thus there are 2^16 equally–likely outcomes.

Each square is divided into 2 triangles. (For example, in a square with vertices A (top–left), B (top–right), C (bottom–right) and D (bottom–left): if you draw the X–diagonal from A to C then one triangle is △ABC and the other is △ACD.) In the whole grid the 32 triangles meet along edges (some of which are “internal” – shared by two triangles – and some lie on the boundary). We wish to know for which diagonal–configurations it is possible to assign one of two “colors” (say 0 and 1) to each triangle so that any two triangles which share an edge get opposite colors. (In graph–theory language, the “dual graph” on the 32 regions is bipartite if and only if such a 2–coloring exists.)

(2) A “Potential–function” Approach

A useful idea is to “assign a base color” to each square in such a way that the colors of the two triangles in that square are then determined by both the square’s base color and the type of diagonal drawn. (One may think of “choosing a base” in each square as a way of “breaking the symmetry” so that when two squares share an edge the colors forced on that edge from the two sides can be compared.)

For example, one may agree on the following rule. In any square choose one of the two triangles to be “base” (for instance, the one touching the top edge) and declare its color to be some bit b (0 or 1). Then define the colors in that square as follows:
 • If the square’s diagonal is drawn as an X (from top–left to bottom–right) then
  – the triangle touching the top edge gets color b,
  – the triangle touching the right edge also gets color b,
  – the triangle touching the bottom edge gets 1–b,
  – the triangle touching the left edge gets 1–b.
 • If instead the square’s diagonal is drawn as a Y (from top–right to bottom–left) then
  – the triangle touching the top edge gets color b,
  – the triangle touching the left edge gets color b,
  – the triangle touching the bottom edge gets 1–b,
  – the triangle touching the right edge gets 1–b.

Now, when two squares share an edge the two triangles that lie along that edge (one from each square) must receive opposite colors. A short check shows that if two squares in the same row share a vertical edge then the rule forces a relation between their base colors that depends on whether the two squares have the same type of diagonal or different ones. (A similar analysis works for vertically adjacent squares.) In fact one may show that a necessary and sufficient condition for a global 2–coloring of all 32 regions to exist is that the following holds:

  For every pair of horizontally adjacent squares the “base colors” must be equal if the two squares have the same diagonal type and opposite if they have different types; and for every pair of vertically adjacent squares the base colors must be equal.

(3) Reformulating the Condition

It turns out that one may “encode” the base–color choices by a 4×4 array of bits b₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ (one for each square). The vertical condition forces that in each column all four entries are equal. (That is, if you label the common value in column j by cⱼ then b₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = cⱼ for every row i.) Then the horizontal condition (when written in “mod 2” language) becomes: for every row i and for every adjacent pair of columns j and j+1 one must have

  cⱼ + c₍ⱼ₊₁₎ = d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎  (mod 2),

where d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ is 0 or 1 according as the square in row i, column j has an X–diagonal or a Y–diagonal. But since the right–hand side must be independent of i, one deduces that for each adjacent pair of columns (j, j+1) the “sum” d₍₁,ⱼ₎+d₍₁,ⱼ₊₁₎ must equal d₍₂,ⱼ₎+d₍₂,ⱼ₊₁₎ and so on (for all 4 rows).

(4) Counting the “Good” Outcomes

Now, note that the only restrictions come from comparing diagonals in adjacent columns. (There is no condition “vertically” because the vertical rule forces all squares in a column to have the same base color.) One may count as follows. First, choose the 4 entries in the first column arbitrarily; there are 2⁴ = 16 choices. Then, for each subsequent column j+1 (j = 1,2,3) the condition forces that in every row the bit in column j+1 is determined by the bit in column j up to a single binary choice (namely, whether d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ equals d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ or its complement). In other words, once column j is chosen there are 2 choices for column j+1. Thus the total number of diagonal–assignments that yield a “compatible” system (and hence a bipartite dual graph, i.e. a 2–coloring of the 32 regions) is

  16 × 2³ = 128.

Since there are 2^16 = 65,536 total outcomes, the desired probability is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be two–colored so that any two regions sharing an edge receive different colors is

  1/512.

This is the answer.

We will show that if one draws, in each of the 16 unit‐squares of a 4×4 board, one of the two possible diagonals (each with probability ½, independently), then the 32 resulting triangular regions can be “two‐colored” (red and blue, with adjacent regions getting different colors) if and only if the 16 “cell–data” (that is, the 16 choices of diagonal in the 16 cells) satisfy a certain “consistency condition.” In the end one may prove that among all 2^16 possible configurations the “good” ones number exactly 128, so the desired probability is

  128/2^16 = 128/65536 = 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
An Outline of One Solution

(1) Associate to each cell a “label” d = 0 or 1 according as its diagonal is drawn from the top‐left to bottom–right (“\”) or from the top–right to bottom–left (“/”). (Thus each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently with probability ½.)

(2) Notice that in any cell the drawn diagonal splits the square into two triangles which share that diagonal as a common edge. (Thus the two triangles in one cell must get opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring.) Also, two triangles in different cells become “neighbors” (i.e. share a whole edge) only along a common side of two adjacent cells.

(3) For convenience, label the cells by coordinates (i,j) with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ 4. In a given cell the four vertices are
  A = (i,j), B = (i,j+1), C = (i+1,j+1), D = (i+1,j).
A short check shows that if the cell’s diagonal is “\” (that is, d = 0) then the triangle with vertices A,B,C touches the top and right sides of the cell while the other triangle (with vertices A,C,D) touches the left and bottom sides. If instead d = 1 (the “/–diagonal”) then the triangle with vertices A,B,D touches the top and left sides while the other (with vertices B,D,C) touches the right and bottom sides.

(4) Now “mark” one of the two triangles in every cell. (For example, in every cell choose the triangle that touches the top edge.) Then assign to that triangle a “color–variable” x (which may be 0 for red and 1 for blue). Since the two triangles in one cell must get opposite colors the other triangle’s color is then forced to be 1–x.

(5) Next, look at an edge shared by two adjacent cells. There are two kinds:

  • A vertical common edge (the right edge of a cell and the left edge of its neighbor to the right). A short check shows that if the left cell has d = 0 then the triangle along its right edge is the “marked” one (so its color is x) while if d = 1 then the marked triangle is not on that edge (so the “unmarked” one, with color 1–x, appears). In the right cell the situation is reversed. In other words, if the left cell has d = 0 and the right cell has d = 0 then the colors on the common edge (one coming from x in the left cell and one coming from 1–x in the right cell) must be opposite; if one cell has d = 0 and the other d = 1 then the roles are interchanged. In all cases one may show that the condition for the two regions along a vertical edge to get opposite colors is
   x_left + x_right = d_left + d_right   (mod 2).

  • A horizontal common edge (the bottom edge of a cell above and the top edge of the cell below). A similar check shows that if the top cell has d = 0 then the triangle along its bottom edge is the “unmarked” one (so its color is 1–x) while if d = 1 then it is the marked one (color x); hence the condition becomes
   x_top + x_bottom = d_top   (mod 2).

(6) One may now “propagate” the color–variables from cell to cell. (For example, using the horizontal conditions one may show that in any given column the color in the cell in row i is determined by that in row 1 plus the “sum” of the d–values in the cells of that column above it.) In the end one finds that a solution (i.e. a proper 2–coloring of all 32 regions) exists if and only if the following “consistency conditions” hold:
  For each vertical pair of adjacent columns (j and j+1, for j = 1,2,3) the “edge–conditions” in the four rows must be compatible. In fact one may show that a solution exists if and only if for every j = 1,2,3 one has
   d_{1,j} ⊕ d_{1,j+1} = d_{2,j} ⊕ d_{2,j+1} = d_{3,j} ⊕ d_{3,j+1} = d_{4,j} ⊕ d_{4,j+1},
where “⊕” denotes addition mod 2.

(7) One may now count. (A short – though not entirely trivial – exercise in “global counting” shows that among all 2^16 possible choices for the 16 d–values exactly 128 yield a system of “edge–conditions” that is consistent.) Hence the probability that a random drawing yields a bipartite (2–colorable) arrangement is

  128/2^16 = 128/65536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

Thus, the answer to the problem is

  1/512.

An answer in brief: The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is 1/512.

We will show that if you label each cell’s diagonal by a 0 or 1 (say, 0 for the “\” diagonal and 1 for the “/” diagonal) then one may prove that the 32 regions (each cell is cut into 2 triangles) can be 2–colored (red/blue so that neighboring regions get different colors) if and only if the 16 numbers (one per cell) satisfy a certain “local‐parity” condition. In fact, one may prove that the dual graph (with a vertex for each triangle and an edge for every common side) is bipartite exactly when for every “2×2 block” of cells the sum (mod 2) of the four entries is 0. (One may show that these 2×2 conditions are equivalent to the existence of a 2–coloring.)

To explain a little more, number the rows and columns 1,…,4 and denote by xᵢ,ⱼ the “type” of the diagonal in cell (i,j) (with xᵢ,ⱼ = 0 if the diagonal is “\” and xᵢ,ⱼ = 1 if it is “/”). Then one may prove that a necessary and sufficient condition for the 32 regions to be 2–colorable is that for every 2×2 block of cells (that is, for every i = 1,…,3 and j = 1,…,3)
  xᵢ,ⱼ + xᵢ,ⱼ₊₁ + xᵢ₊₁,ⱼ + xᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₊₁ ≡ 0 (mod 2).
(There is a nice “local–to–global” argument behind this fact; see, for example, discussions of “random diagonals” in a grid.)

Now, since there are 4×4 = 16 cells the total number of configurations is 2¹⁶ = 65,536. (Each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently at random.) One may show by a short linear–algebra argument over GF(2) that the 9 equations (one for each 2×2 block) are not all independent but in fact have
  rank = (3×3) – (2×2) = 9 – 4 = 5.
That is, the 9 equations impose 5 independent conditions on the 16 variables. (You can check that for a 2×2 grid the unique equation is independent and for a 3×3 grid the 4 equations have rank 3.) Hence the number of “good” configurations (those for which all the 2×2 sums vanish mod 2) is

  2^(16 – 5) = 2¹¹ = 2048.

Thus the desired probability is

  2048 / 65,536 = 1/32.

So the answer is 1/32.

We will show that no “exotic” 2‐coloring is possible unless every one of the 16 unit squares is “cut” in the same way. (In other words, if you label the two possible diagonals 0 and 1 then a valid red–blue coloring of all 32 triangles exists only when every cell has the same label.) Since each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently (with 2 choices per cell) there are 2^16 total configurations and only 2 of these (all 0’s or all 1’s) yield a “bipartite” arrangement. Hence the desired probability is

  2⁄2^16 = 1⁄2^15 = 1⁄32768.

Below is one way to explain this result.

──────────────────────────────
An Explanation

Suppose you have a 4×4 grid. In each unit square a diagonal is drawn; there are two possibilities. (For convenience, label the two choices 0 and 1.) In any given square the diagonal divides it into two triangles. (For example, if we label the four vertices of a square as top‐left (TL), top‐right (TR), bottom‐right (BR) and bottom‐left (BL), then one diagonal is TL–BR and the other is TR–BL.)

Now, note that although the two triangles in one square share the diagonal, they do not share a full edge (an edge is a side of a square, not just a portion of it). Thus the only “neighbor‐relations” occur along the sides common to two adjacent squares. (There are 32 regions in all.)

For a fixed square the way its diagonal is drawn determines exactly which triangle “claims” each side. (For example, if the diagonal is TL–BR then the triangle with vertices TL, TR, BR touches the top and right sides, while the other triangle touches the bottom and left sides. If instead the diagonal is TR–BL then the triangle with vertices TL, TR, BL touches the top and left sides, while the other touches the bottom and right sides.)

Now suppose you wish to color the 32 regions red and blue so that any two regions which share a full edge get different colors. (This is equivalent to saying that the “dual graph” whose vertices are the regions is bipartite.) One may show by “propagating” the color–choice from one square to its neighbor that the color forced on the triangle lying along a common edge depends only on the diagonal–choice in that square. (In fact one may “fix” a coloring in one square and then, using the condition on every common edge, show that the color forced on the triangle in a neighboring square is determined by that neighbor’s diagonal–choice.)

A short analysis shows that if you label the two diagonal choices 0 and 1 then the rule along a common edge forces the following:
 • Along a vertical edge (shared by a square above and one below) the “color” forced on the common edge is, say, “blue” if the top square is 0 and “red” if it is 1. (One may check this by drawing a picture.) In order for the two regions on opposite sides of the edge to receive opposite colors the bottom square must “agree” with the top one – that is, it too must be 0 (if the top is 0) or 1 (if the top is 1).
 • A similar analysis along a horizontal edge shows that the two horizontally adjacent squares must have the same label.

Since the grid is connected (every square touches some other along an edge) it follows that in order to be able to assign colors to all 32 regions consistently the label in every square must be the same. (In other words, a valid 2–coloring exists only when every cell is cut by the same diagonal.)

There are 2^16 total ways to choose the diagonals but only 2 of these (all 0’s or all 1’s) yield a “bipartite” arrangement. Therefore the desired probability is

  2⁄2^16 = 1⁄2^15 = 1⁄32768.
──────────────────────────────

Thus, the answer is 1/32768.

We will show that if we choose a diagonal (either “\” or “/”) independently and uniformly at random in each of the 16 cells of a 4×4 grid, then the 32 triangles formed can be 2‐colored (red/blue with neighboring regions opposite in color) if and only if a certain “global” condition holds – and a short counting argument shows that this happens with probability 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Modeling Each Cell

Label the rows 1,…,4 (top to bottom) and the columns 1,…,4 (left to right). In each cell we choose one of the two diagonals. It is convenient to “encode” the choice by a bit:
  • Let d = 0 mean we draw the “\” diagonal (from the top‐left to bottom‐right).
  • Let d = 1 mean we draw the “/” diagonal (from the top‐right to bottom‐left).

In a given square the diagonal splits the cell into 2 triangles. (For example, if the cell’s vertices are A (top‐left), B (top‐right), C (bottom‐right), D (bottom‐left), then with a “\” diagonal the two triangles are △ABC and △ACD; with a “/” diagonal they are △ABD and △BCD.)

An important observation is that the two triangles in the same cell share the drawn diagonal as a common edge. (They meet along a full segment, not just at a point.) Therefore, in any proper red–blue coloring the two triangles in one cell must receive opposite colors.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Describing the “Edge‐Sharing” Conditions

Apart from the diagonal inside each cell, some triangles in neighboring cells share a boundary segment. (Only segments of positive length count; triangles that meet only at a point are not “neighbors” for our coloring.)

It turns out that one may check by a short case–analysis that if we “mark” in each cell which of its two triangles touches a given side then the answers are as follows:

• For a cell with d = 0 (“\”):
  – The top edge is touched by triangle 1.
  – The right edge is touched by triangle 1.
  – The bottom edge is touched by triangle 2.
  – The left edge is touched by triangle 2.

• For a cell with d = 1 (“/”):
  – The top edge is touched by triangle 1.
  – The left edge is touched by triangle 1.
  – The bottom edge is touched by triangle 2.
  – The right edge is touched by triangle 2.

Now, when two cells share a common edge the “neighboring” triangles are determined as follows. (For example, consider two horizontally adjacent cells in the same row. The right edge of the left cell and the left edge of the right cell are common.)
  – In a “\” cell the right edge is triangle 1 while in a “/” cell the left edge is triangle 1.
  – In a “\” cell the left edge is triangle 2 while in a “/” cell the right edge is triangle 2.

A similar analysis works for vertical neighbors. (For vertical edges the roles of “left” and “right” are interchanged.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Setting Up a “Binary Variable” per Cell

Since in each cell the two triangles must get opposite colors, we may “encode” the coloring in each cell by a binary variable x:
  • In a given cell, declare that x = 0 means “triangle 1 is red (and triangle 2 blue)” and x = 1 means “triangle 1 is blue (and triangle 2 red).”

One may check that with this convention the color of the triangle touching a given side depends on both the cell’s diagonal type d and its variable x. For instance:
  – In a “\” cell (d = 0) the right edge is triangle 1 so its color is x.
  – In a “/” cell (d = 1) the right edge is triangle 2 so its color is 1 – x.
A similar rule holds for the other sides.

Now, consider the shared edges between neighboring cells. For example, for two horizontally adjacent cells the condition that the two touching triangles have opposite colors translates into a relation between the x–values in the two cells. (A short check shows that the horizontal (top–bottom) neighbors force the x–value in a given column to be the same in every cell of that column.)

In fact, one may show that the horizontal edges force that in every column the x–value is constant. (Call the common value in column j “y_j”.) Then the vertical edges (between cells in the same row) impose a condition that relates the y–values in adjacent columns. In particular, if you work through the cases you find that for a given row the following must hold for j = 1, 2, 3:
  • If the two adjacent cells in that row have the same diagonal (d = 0 in both or d = 1 in both) then the condition forces y_j = y_(j+1).
  • If they have different diagonals then the condition forces y_j ≠ y_(j+1).

But note: the y–values (one for each column) are global (the same for every row). Therefore, for the entire grid to admit a proper 2–coloring the condition coming from every row must “agree.” In other words, if in row i we define
  δ_i(j) = 0 if d(i,j) = d(i,j+1), and δ_i(j) = 1 if d(i,j) ≠ d(i,j+1)
(for j = 1, 2, 3),
then there must exist a fixed “global difference sequence” Δ = (Δ(1), Δ(2), Δ(3)) (with each Δ(j) ∈ {0,1}) so that for every row i and every j we have
  δ_i(j) = Δ(j).

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Counting the “Good” Configurations

How many ways can a given row’s four diagonal–choices produce a prescribed difference sequence Δ? (Remember that each row’s four cells are chosen independently from {0,1}.) Once you know the value in the first cell (2 choices), the remaining three are forced by the differences. Thus for any fixed Δ there are exactly 2 assignments in that row that yield it. Since there are 2³ = 8 possible difference sequences Δ, a given row has 2×8 = 16 assignments – as expected.

Now, for the whole grid to be “good” (i.e. to admit a 2–coloring) all four rows must produce the same difference sequence Δ. The first row may be arbitrary (16 possibilities), but then each subsequent row must “match” the first row’s Δ. Since for any fixed row the probability that its four cells yield a prescribed Δ is 2/16 = 1/8, the probability that rows 2, 3, and 4 all match row 1 is
  (1/8)³ = 1/512.

Since there are 2^16 = 65536 total configurations (each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently), the number of “good” configurations is
  (1/512) × 65536 = 128.
Thus the desired probability is 128/65536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is

  1/512.

We will show that if one places a diagonal (one of the two possible ones) in each cell of a 4×4 grid at random, then the 32 little triangles obtained can be 2‐colored (red/blue with adjacent regions opposite in color) exactly when a certain “column–relation” holds. In fact, one may prove that a proper 2–coloring exists if and only if for every pair of adjacent columns the “diagonal–pattern” in the two columns is “uniform” – that is, in every row the two diagonals are either both of the same type or both of opposite types. (One may show that then the “vertical” edge–conditions force a consistent choice of colors.) A short counting shows that the probability of this happening is 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setting Up the Problem

Label the rows 1,…,4 and the columns 1,…,4. In each cell we choose one of the two diagonals uniformly at random. (Thus there are 2^16 total configurations.) In any given square the diagonal splits the cell into two triangles. (For example, if we label the vertices of a cell as NW, NE, SE, SW then one may choose the NW–SE diagonal so that the triangle with vertices NW, NE, SE gets the top and right sides, while the other triangle (NW, SW, SE) gets the left and bottom sides. Alternatively, choosing the NE–SW diagonal yields one triangle (NW, NE, SW) having the top and left sides and the other (NE, SE, SW) having the right and bottom sides.)

In every cell the two triangles share the diagonal as a common edge; hence they must receive opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring. (We will refer to “coloring” as assigning “red” and “blue” to the regions.)

Next, note that two triangular regions in different cells will be adjacent (i.e. share a full edge) only when a whole side of one cell is also a side of the adjacent cell. (For instance, the right side of a cell and the left side of its neighbor form a common edge.) A short check shows that in every cell the diagonal “chooses” which triangle gets which of the four sides. (For example, in a cell with the NW–SE diagonal the triangle having the top edge is unique, and so is the one having the bottom edge; similarly for a cell with the NE–SW diagonal.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Encoding the “Local” Data

For convenience we now “mark” in each cell the unique triangle that touches the top edge. (One may check that no matter which diagonal is chosen, there is exactly one triangle in the cell that has the top side as one of its boundaries.) Now, in any cell the other triangle (the one not touching the top) must get the opposite color. (That is forced by the fact that the two triangles in a cell share the diagonal.)

Thus if we denote by c the color (say, 0 for red and 1 for blue) assigned to the top–edge triangle in a given cell, then the “other” triangle gets color 1–c.

Now, look at what happens along a common edge between two adjacent cells. There are two types:

• A vertical common edge (the right edge of the left cell and the left edge of the right cell).  
• A horizontal common edge (the bottom edge of the top cell and the top edge of the bottom cell).

A short check shows that the horizontal edges force no extra condition (apart from the obvious fact that the top–edge color in a cell must be the same as that in the cell immediately above it). (In fact, if the top–edge color in the top cell is c then the bottom–edge color in that cell is 1–c and the top–edge color in the cell below is forced to equal c in order for the common horizontal edge to join regions of opposite colors.)

The vertical edges are the real “obstacle.” To explain this, note that in a given cell the diagonal “chooses” which triangle touches which side. In fact one may check that if we denote by d the “type” of the diagonal in a cell (say, 0 for NW–SE and 1 for NE–SW) then the following holds:
 
 – In a cell with d = 0 (NW–SE):  
  • The triangle touching the top edge gets color c (by our choice)  
  • The triangle touching the right edge also gets color c, while  
  • The triangle touching the left edge gets color 1–c, and  
  • The triangle touching the bottom edge gets color 1–c.

 – In a cell with d = 1 (NE–SW):  
  • The triangle touching the top edge gets color c,  
  • The triangle touching the left edge gets color c, while  
  • The triangle touching the right edge gets color 1–c, and  
  • The triangle touching the bottom edge gets color 1–c.

Now, consider a vertical edge between two adjacent cells in columns j and j+1. This common edge is the right edge of the left cell and the left edge of the right cell. In the left cell the triangle touching the right edge has color:
  • c if d = 0,  
  • 1–c if d = 1.
In the right cell the triangle touching the left edge has color:
  • 1–c if d = 0,  
  • c if d = 1.

For the two regions sharing the vertical edge to have opposite colors the following must hold (working in ℤ₂):
  [Color in left cell] + [Color in right cell] = 1.
A short check shows that this forces a relation between the “column–choices” a_j (the common top–edge color in column j) and the diagonal types in the two cells. In fact one finds that for each row i the condition is:
  if the two cells have the same d–value then a_j must equal a_{j+1},
  if they have opposite d–values then a_j must differ from a_{j+1}.

Since the top–edge color in a given column is the same for all its cells (by the horizontal condition) the vertical edge condition “across” a pair of adjacent columns forces that for every row the relation between the d–values in the two columns is the same. In other words, for each adjacent pair of columns (say, columns j and j+1) one must have either
  for every row i: d_{ij} = d_{i,j+1}                                                                                                                             (1)
or
  for every row i: d_{ij} ≠ d_{i,j+1}.                                                                                                                             (2)

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Counting the “Good” Configurations

Now, view the 4×4 array of cells as 4 columns (each column being a 4–bit vector giving the d–values in that column). There is no restriction on the first column (16 choices). But for each adjacent pair of columns the “good” condition is that the two 4–bit vectors are either identical or complementary (component–wise). (For a fixed pair of columns the chance that in a given row the two entries are equal is ½ and that they are different is ½; so for all 4 rows to be equal the probability is (½)^4 = 1/16 and similarly for all 4 to be different it is 1/16. Thus for a given adjacent pair the probability is 2/16 = 1/8.)

Since there are 3 pairs of adjacent columns (columns 1–2, 2–3, and 3–4) the total probability that a random configuration satisfies the needed condition is
  (1/8) × (1/8) × (1/8) = 1/512.

An equivalent way to count is to note that once the first column is chosen (16 choices) each subsequent column is forced to be either equal to or the complement of the previous column. Thus the number of “good” matrices is
  16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 128,
and since the total number of matrices is 16^4 = 65,536, the probability is 128/65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Conclusion

A proper 2–coloring of the 32 regions exists (i.e. the regions can be colored red and blue so that any two sharing an edge have different colors) if and only if for every pair of adjacent columns the 4 entries (one per row) in one column are either all equal to or all different from the corresponding entries in the neighboring column. A short counting shows that this happens with probability 1/512.

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability is 1/512.

We will show that if one puts a diagonal (either “\” or “/”) in each of the 16 unit‐cells of a 4×4 board (so there are 2^16 total drawings), then the 32 little triangles obtained can be “two–colored” (red/blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have opposite colors) if and only if a certain “global parity condition” holds. In fact, one may prove that exactly 128 of the 2^16 = 65,536 drawings yield a “bipartite” dual graph (the graph whose vertices are the 32 regions, with an edge joining two regions that share a side) and hence the desired probability is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A way to “see” the answer

(1) Partitioning each cell.
 Each cell is a unit square. In it one draws one of the two diagonals. (For definiteness, label the two diagonals as “\” and “/”.) This splits the cell into two triangles. (For example, if the cell’s vertices are labeled bottom‐left, bottom–right, top–right, and top–left then with the “\” diagonal the two triangles are
  • triangle with vertices bottom–left, bottom–right, top–right (touching the bottom and right sides) and 
  • triangle with vertices bottom–left, top–left, top–right (touching the left and top sides). 
A similar description holds for the “/” diagonal.)

(2) Forming the dual graph.
 Now, “regions” means the 32 triangles. Two regions are declared adjacent if they share a whole segment (not merely a point). (Note that the common boundary between two cells is a full edge of a cell, and the drawn diagonal in a cell meets that edge in exactly one point; so on a common edge the two cells contribute one little edge each to the boundary between two triangles.) One may show that the condition “any two regions sharing an edge have different colors” is equivalent to saying that the graph whose vertices are the regions and whose edges connect regions sharing an edge is bipartite.

(3) A “local‐to–global” reformulation.
 A very nice way to attack the problem is to “decorate” each cell by choosing an arbitrary “base color” (say, 0 or 1) and then “adjusting” the color on the side where the diagonal meets the boundary. (In any cell the diagonal splits the square so that one of the two triangles touches the right and bottom edges and the other touches the left and top edges. In our picture one may check that if we declare that in a cell with “\” the triangle touching the right (or bottom) edge gets the “base color” and the one touching the left (or top) edge gets the opposite color, while in a cell with “/” the roles are reversed, then one may “propagate” a 2–coloring of the regions provided that on every common edge the two “adjusted” colors are opposites.)

More precisely, one may show that if we label the cells by coordinates (i,j) (with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ 4) and write d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = 0 when the cell’s diagonal is “\” and 1 when it is “/”, then a short analysis shows that the condition for a 2–coloring to exist is equivalent to the following:
 For every row i the “horizontal differences”
  d₍ᵢ,₁₎ + d₍ᵢ,₂₎, d₍ᵢ,₂₎ + d₍ᵢ,₃₎, d₍ᵢ,₃₎ + d₍ᵢ,₄₎
must all equal the same triple (c₁, c₂, c₃) (where the addition is mod 2) independent of i.

(To explain a little more: One may “imagine” that if one were to choose a base color for each cell then the condition that adjacent regions get opposite colors forces (after a short check) that on every common horizontal edge the “sum” d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ must be the same for every row. In other words, if in row i the equation
  d₍ᵢ,₁₎ + d₍ᵢ,₂₎ = c₁, d₍ᵢ,₂₎ + d₍ᵢ,₃₎ = c₂, d₍ᵢ,₃₎ + d₍ᵢ,₄₎ = c₃
holds (with c₁, c₂, c₃ ∈ {0,1}), then the same triple (c₁, c₂, c₃) must work in every row.)

(4) Counting the “good” configurations.
 Now, fix an arbitrary triple (c₁, c₂, c₃) ∈ {0,1}³. Look at one row. The three equations
  d₍ᵢ,₁₎ + d₍ᵢ,₂₎ = c₁,
  d₍ᵢ,₂₎ + d₍ᵢ,₃₎ = c₂,
  d₍ᵢ,₃₎ + d₍ᵢ,₄₎ = c₃
are linear (mod 2) in the 4 unknowns d₍ᵢ,₁₎, d₍ᵢ,₂₎, d₍ᵢ,₃₎, d₍ᵢ,₄₎. One may check that for any given (c₁, c₂, c₃) there are exactly 2 solutions in {0,1}⁴. (In other words, in each row the 4–tuple (d₍ᵢ,₁₎, d₍ᵢ,₂₎, d₍ᵢ,₃₎, d₍ᵢ,₄₎) is forced to lie in one of 8 disjoint affine subspaces of F₂⁴, and exactly one of these 8 subspaces will yield the prescribed triple of sums.)
 Since the rows are independent, if we insist that every row have the same prescribed triple (c₁, c₂, c₃) then there are 2⁴ possibilities (one for each row). Since there are 2³ = 8 choices for (c₁, c₂, c₃), the total number of “good” configurations is
  8 × 2⁴ = 128.

(5) The final probability.
 Since there are 2^16 = 65,536 total configurations, the probability that a random drawing is “good” (i.e. its 32 regions can be two–colored properly) is
  128/65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Answer

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1/512.

An answer in brief:
 The probability is 1/512.

We will show that if we label each cell by a 0–1 variable according to which diagonal is drawn, then the 32 regions can be 2–colored (with “red” and “blue”) if and only if a certain system of 9 “parity‐conditions” (one for each interior vertex of the grid) is satisfied. In the end one may prove that exactly 2⁸ of the 2¹⁶ possible choices yield a “good” (bipartite) picture – so the desired probability is

  2⁸⁄2¹⁶ = 256⁄65536 = 1⁄256.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “Model” for the Problem

Imagine a 4×4 array of unit squares. In each square one of the two diagonals is drawn at random. (There are 2 choices per cell, so 2¹⁶ total outcomes.) Each drawn diagonal splits its square into 2 triangles; altogether there are 32 regions. We wish to know for which choices of diagonals it is possible to “2–color” the regions (say, red and blue) so that any two regions sharing an entire edge (not merely a point) have different colors. (In graph–theory language, the dual graph of the regions is bipartite.)

It turns out that the only potential obstructions to 2–coloring come from “odd cycles” in the dual graph. In our picture such cycles occur “around” the interior vertices (the points where four cells meet). (On the boundary no cycle is “closed” in the dual graph.) Thus one may show that a necessary and sufficient condition for the dual graph to be bipartite is that at every interior vertex the following holds.

──────────────────────────────
The Local Condition

Label the 16 cells by coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i, j ≤ 4. In each cell choose a variable

  xᵢⱼ = 0 if the NW–SE diagonal is drawn, and
  xᵢⱼ = 1 if the NE–SW diagonal is drawn.

Now, focus on an interior vertex. (There are 9 of these since the grid has 5×5 vertices and the boundary ones are excluded.) For example, consider the interior vertex common to the four cells in positions
  (top‐left) (i–1, j–1),
  (top–right) (i–1, j),
  (bottom–left) (i, j–1),
  (bottom–right) (i, j),
with 2 ≤ i, j ≤ 4.

Notice that in a given square the diagonal “hits” the vertex if and only if the vertex is one of its endpoints. (A NW–SE diagonal runs from the top–left to the bottom–right corner; a NE–SW diagonal runs from the top–right to the bottom–left.) Thus, at the common vertex the following happens:
 • In cell (i–1, j–1) the vertex is the bottom–right corner, so it is hit if and only if xᵢ₋₁,ⱼ₋₁ = 0.
 • In cell (i–1, j) the vertex is the bottom–left corner, so it is hit if and only if xᵢ₋₁,ⱼ = 1.
 • In cell (i, j–1) the vertex is the top–right corner, so it is hit if and only if xᵢ,ⱼ₋₁ = 1.
 • In cell (i, j) the vertex is the top–left corner, so it is hit if and only if xᵢ,ⱼ = 0.

One may show that a “parity‐check” at the vertex is equivalent to requiring that the total number of cells (among these four) whose diagonal passes through the vertex is even. In other words, for each interior vertex (with “top–left” cell (i–1, j–1)) we must have

We will show that if one places a diagonal (one of the two possible ones) in each cell of a 4×4 grid at random, then the 32 resulting triangular regions can be “two‐colored” (red/blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have opposite colors) if and only if the diagonals in the grid “line up” in a very special way. In fact, one may prove that a necessary and sufficient condition is that for every pair of horizontally adjacent cells the “pattern” of diagonals in the two cells is “the same” or “completely opposite” in every row. (A similar statement holds for vertical neighbors, but as you will see the horizontal conditions force the answer.) A short counting argument then shows that the number of “good” outcomes is

  (Number of valid outcomes) = (choices for column 1) × (2 choices for each transition)
                 = 2⁴ · 2³ = 16·8 = 128.

Since there are 16 cells and each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently (with 2 choices per cell) the total number of outcomes is 2¹⁶ = 65,536. Hence the desired probability is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

To explain a little more in detail, here is one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
A Sample Explanation

(1) In each cell a diagonal is drawn. There are two types:
  • Type “\” (we call this d = 0) divides the cell into a “top‐left” triangle (which touches the top and left edges) and a “bottom‐right” triangle (which touches the bottom and right edges).
  • Type “/” (we call this d = 1) divides the cell into a “top‐right” triangle (touching the top and right edges) and a “bottom‐left” triangle (touching the bottom and left edges).

Since the two triangles in one cell share the drawn diagonal, they must get opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring.

(2) Now look at two cells that share a common edge. For example, consider two horizontally adjacent cells. In the left cell the right edge is touched by:
  – the bottom‐right triangle if the cell has a “\” (d = 0),
  – the top‐right triangle if the cell has a “/” (d = 1).
In the right cell the left edge is touched by:
  – the top‐left triangle if that cell has a “\” (d = 0),
  – the bottom‐left triangle if that cell has a “/” (d = 1).

A short check shows that in order for the colors on these two touching edges to be opposite, one must have a certain relation between the “types” (d–values) in the two cells. (A similar analysis works for vertically adjacent cells.)

(3) One may show that after one makes a clever choice of “base” triangles (for example, always taking the triangle that touches the top edge of its cell) the only way to “patch together” a 2–coloring of all 32 regions is to have the following property: For every pair of horizontally adjacent cells the “difference” between the diagonals in the two cells is the same in every row. In other words, if you label the cells in column j by their d–value (0 or 1) then for every j = 1, 2, 3 the 4 “differences”
  d(i,j) ⊕ d(i,j+1)  (for i = 1,…,4)
must all be equal (all 0’s or all 1’s).

(4) Now, notice that if you “read” the grid by its columns the condition is equivalent to saying that for each j = 1, 2, 3 the (entire) (j+1)st column is either identical to the jth column or is its bit–wise complement. (There is no restriction vertically because one may always choose the colors on the top edges of each column independently.) Since each column has 4 bits the first column can be chosen in 2⁴ = 16 ways, and then for each of the three transitions (from column 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and 3 to 4) there are 2 choices (either “same” or “complement”). Thus the total number of “good” outcomes is 16 · 2³ = 128.

(5) Since the total number of outcomes is 2¹⁶ = 65,536 the desired probability is 128/65,536 = 1/512.
──────────────────────────────

Thus, the answer to the problem is 1/512.

We will show that if you choose a diagonal in each of the 16 unit squares of a 4×4 grid at random (each square’s diagonal is chosen independently with equal probability for the “\” or “/” orientation), then the 32 resulting triangles can be 2‐colored (red/blue so that neighboring regions share different colors) with probability

  1/2^( (4–1)² ) = 1/2^9 = 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way of “seeing” why the answer is 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
A “Heuristic” Explanation

1. Setup. Label the rows 1,…,4 and columns 1,…,4. In each unit square (cell) the two possible diagonals are drawn. (For example, in a cell with corners A (top‐left), B (top‐right), C (bottom‐right) and D (bottom‐left) one may draw the “\” diagonal joining A and C or the “/” diagonal joining B and D.) In either case the cell is divided into 2 triangles. (Note that the two triangles in a cell share the drawn diagonal; they are “neighbors” in the final picture.)

2. The Dual Graph. Now form a graph whose vertices correspond to the 32 triangles and in which two vertices are joined by an edge exactly when the corresponding triangles share a full side (that is, a side that is not just a point). One may check that the “internal” edge (the drawn diagonal in a cell) always joins the two triangles in that cell. In addition, triangles in adjacent cells may share a side along a common edge of the grid. (For instance, if two horizontally adjacent cells both have their “\” diagonal then the triangle in the left cell that touches its right edge is adjacent to the triangle in the right cell that touches its left edge.)

3. Bipartiteness. A necessary and sufficient condition for being able to 2‐color the regions (so that adjacent regions get different colors) is that the dual graph is bipartite (i.e. it contains no odd cycles).

4. A Height–Function Interpretation. One may show that by “marking” each cell with a +1 (if its diagonal is “\”) or –1 (if it is “/”) one may assign “heights” to the vertices of the grid in such a way that the condition for the dual graph to be bipartite is equivalent to a collection of “cycle–conditions.” In fact, one may prove that a necessary and sufficient condition is that for every closed loop (cycle) made up of grid–edges the product of the signs (i.e. the “twists”) is +1. (One way to think of this is that a failure of this condition produces an odd cycle in the dual graph.)

5. Counting the Constraints. It turns out that in an n×n grid the number of independent “cycle–conditions” is (n–1)². (For n = 4 there are 9 independent conditions.) Since each cell’s diagonal is chosen at random (giving a “flip” of sign with probability ½), the probability that all (n–1)² conditions are met is 1/2^((n–1)²). For n = 4 this is 1/2^9 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
A Quick Check in a Smaller Case

To build some intuition, one may check the 2×2 case. There the number of independent conditions is (2–1)² = 1 so the probability would be 1/2. (A short case–check shows that exactly half of the 16 possible 2×2 configurations yield a bipartite dual graph.) This is consistent with the general answer.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Thus, for a 4×4 grid the probability that the 32 triangular regions (formed by drawing one diagonal in each cell at random) can be 2–colored (red and blue with adjacent regions of different colors) is

  1/2^9 = 1/512.

So the final answer is 1/512.

We will show that if you choose a diagonal (one of the two) in each of the 16 cells independently and uniformly at random, then the 32 resulting triangles can be 2‐colored (red/blue with adjacent regions opposite in color) if and only if the 4×4 array of “diagonal–choices” has a very special form. In fact, one may prove that a valid 2–coloring exists exactly when the following condition holds:

  For every pair of adjacent columns (that is, for j = 1, 2, 3) the entire column j+1 is either identical to column j or is the exact complement of column j (i.e. in every row the bit in column j+1 is the same as or opposite to the bit in column j).

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this conclusion and then count the number of “good” configurations.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setting Up the Problem

Label the rows 1,…,4 and columns 1,…,4. In each cell (i, j) we draw one of the two diagonals. (There are 2^16 total configurations.) In any given square the drawn diagonal splits the cell into two triangles. (For example, if we label the four corners of a cell as A (top‐left), B (top–right), C (bottom–right), and D (bottom–left), then drawing the “main” diagonal AC gives triangles △ABC and △ACD; drawing the “anti–diagonal” BD gives triangles △ABD and △BCD.)

Now, the 32 triangles form a planar partition of the square. Two triangles “share an edge” if they meet along a full segment (either a segment of the original grid or a segment of one of the drawn diagonals). In particular, note that:
• In every cell the two triangles share the drawn diagonal. Hence they must receive opposite colors.
• If two cells share a side of the grid then the piece of that side that lies in one cell is a side of one of its two triangles and the corresponding piece in the adjacent cell is a side of one of its triangles. Thus the colors on these two triangles must also be opposite.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Convenient Way to Encode the Configuration

For each cell (i, j) let d(i, j) = 0 if the main diagonal (from A to C) is drawn and 1 if the anti–diagonal (from B to D) is drawn.

Now, observe what happens in a given cell. Write the vertices as
  A = top–left, B = top–right, C = bottom–right, D = bottom–left.
Then:
• If d(i, j) = 0 (main diagonal AC is drawn) the two triangles are:
  △ABC (which has sides AB, BC, and AC) and
  △ACD (which has sides AD, CD, and AC).
• If d(i, j) = 1 (anti–diagonal BD is drawn) the two triangles are:
  △ABD (with sides AB, AD, and BD) and
  △BCD (with sides BC, CD, and BD).

Thus in any cell one triangle touches the top edge and one touches the bottom edge. (In a main–diagonal cell the top–edge triangle is △ABC and the bottom–edge triangle is △ACD; in an anti–diagonal cell the top–edge triangle is △ABD and the bottom–edge triangle is △BCD.)

Because the two triangles in a cell share the diagonal they must get opposite colors. (So if we “choose” a color for one triangle then the other is forced.)

Now, let us “mark” each cell by choosing, for convenience, the color of the triangle that touches its top edge. Denote this by x(i, j) (which can be 0 for red and 1 for blue). Then the triangle touching the bottom edge in cell (i, j) gets the opposite color, namely 1 – x(i, j).

Next, let us see which triangle in a cell touches its right or left edge:
• In a cell with d(i, j) = 0 (main diagonal) the triangle touching the top edge (△ABC) also touches the right edge.
• In a cell with d(i, j) = 1 (anti–diagonal) the triangle touching the top edge (△ABD) touches the left edge while the other triangle (△BCD) touches the right edge.

Thus we can “read off” the color on the right edge of cell (i, j) as follows:
  if d(i, j) = 0, then the right edge gets color x(i, j);
  if d(i, j) = 1, then the right edge gets color 1 – x(i, j).

A similar analysis shows that in the cell to the left (say cell (i, j–1)) the left edge’s color is:

  = 1 – x(i, j+1) if d(i, j+1) = 0, or x(i, j+1) if d(i, j+1) = 1.

Step 4. Counting the “Good” Configurations

There are 16 cells so initially there are 2^16 total configurations. However, a necessary and sufficient condition for a valid 2–coloring is that for every adjacent pair of columns (j, j+1) the entire column j+1 equals or is the complement of column j.

• The first column (column 1) is arbitrary; it can be any of 2^4 = 16 4–bit vectors.
• For each subsequent column j+1 (j = 1, 2, 3) once column j is given there are exactly 2 choices: either copy column j or take its complement.
Thus the total number of “good” configurations is
  16 × 2^3 = 16 × 8 = 128.

Since there are 2^16 = 65536 total configurations, the desired probability is
  128 / 65536 = 1/512.

Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is 1/512.
