We will show that if we label each cell’s diagonal by a 0 or 1 (with, say, 0 corresponding to the “\” diagonal and 1 corresponding to the “/” diagonal), then a necessary and sufficient condition for the 32 regions (the two triangles in each cell) to be 2‐colorable (so that any two regions sharing an edge get opposite colors) is that in every 2×2 block of cells the sum (mod 2) of the four entries is 0. (In other words, every 2×2 block must contain an even number of “/” diagonals.) One may show that this “2‐colorability” condition is equivalent to the absence of “odd cycles” in the graph whose vertices are the triangular regions and whose edges join regions that share a side.

Let us explain one way to arrive at this condition and then count the number of “good” assignments.

Step 1. Encoding the Diagonals

Label the cells of the 4×4 grid by coordinates (i, j) with 1 ≤ i, j ≤ 4. In each cell choose a diagonal uniformly at random. Encode the choice by a variable 
  x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ ∈ {0,1},
where we may take 0 to mean “\” and 1 to mean “/”. (Any fixed convention will do.)

Step 2. The 2×2 Condition

A key observation is that if you look at any 2×2 block of cells, the way the diagonals “twist” forces a parity condition on the regions. (You can check by drawing a 2×2 square and “walking” around the central point where the four cells meet that the cycle you obtain has even length if and only if
  x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ + x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ + x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₊₁₎ ≡ 0 (mod 2).)
One may prove that a necessary and sufficient condition for the entire 4×4 arrangement to be 2‐colorable is that every one of the nine 2×2 blocks (there are 3 in each direction) satisfies
  x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + x₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ + x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ + x₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₊₁₎ = 0  (in F₂).

Step 3. Counting the “Good” Assignments

There are 16 cells so a total of 2¹⁶ = 65,536 equally likely assignments of 0’s and 1’s.

Now, the condition we have is a system of 9 linear equations (one for each 2×2 block) in 16 unknowns over the field F₂. (For example, for the upper‐left 2×2 block we have
  x₍₁,₁₎ + x₍₁,₂₎ + x₍₂,₁₎ + x₍₂,₂₎ = 0.)
A short “boundary‐freezing” argument shows that one may choose the values on the first row and the first column (except that the upper‐left cell is counted in both) arbitrarily and then all the remaining 16 – (4 + 3) = 9 cells become determined. (You may verify this by “solving” the 2×2 equations in a 3×3 grid; one finds that the number of solutions is 2^(number of free parameters) with free parameters equal to 3 + 2 = 5. In general, for an n×n grid the number of free parameters turns out to be 2n – 1.) For a 4×4 grid the free parameters are the 4 entries in the first row and the 3 entries in the first column below the first row, a total of 7 free parameters. (A short check in the 2×2 and 3×3 cases shows that the number of “good” assignments is 2³ = 8 for a 2×2 grid and 2⁵ = 32 for a 3×3 grid.) Hence for a 4×4 grid the number of assignments satisfying all the 2×2 conditions is 2⁷ = 128.

Step 4. The Final Probability

Since there are 65,536 total assignments and 128 “good” ones, the desired probability is

  128/65,536 = 1/512.

Thus, the answer is 1/512.

We will show that a valid “red–blue” coloring exists if and only if in every row the “pattern” of diagonals has an even number of “switches” (that is, changes from one type to the other). In a 4×4 grid there are 4 rows and each row (with 4 cells) has 3 “gaps” between adjacent cells. A short counting shows that for any fixed row the probability that the number of changes is even is ½, and since the rows act independently the overall probability is (½)^4 = 1/16.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Setting Up the Problem

In each of the 16 cells we choose one of two diagonals:
• The “\” diagonal (from top‐left to bottom‐right) or 
• The “/” diagonal (from top‐right to bottom‐left).

Thus there are 2^16 equally likely assignments. When a diagonal is drawn the cell is divided into 2 triangles. (In each cell the two triangles share the diagonal as a common edge; hence they must receive opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring.)

We wish to color the 32 resulting triangles red and blue so that any two triangles which share a full edge (whether that edge is part of the cell boundary or is the diagonal inside a cell) have different colors. In graph–theoretic language the “dual graph” whose vertices represent triangles and whose edges represent shared full edges must be bipartite.

──────────────────────────────
Step 2. A Convenient “Bookkeeping” Device

A very useful idea is to “mark” each cell by choosing one of its two triangles and declaring its color (say, 0 for red and 1 for blue). (Because the two triangles in a cell must get opposite colors, once you choose the color for one triangle the other is forced.) It turns out that one may consistently choose, in every cell, the triangle that touches the north edge. (Of course, which triangle touches the north edge depends on the diagonal drawn.)

To be precise, label the vertices of a cell as follows:
  A = top–left, B = top–right, C = bottom–right, D = bottom–left.
Then:
• If the cell’s diagonal is “\” (from A to C) the two triangles are △ABC and △ACD. In this case the north edge AB belongs to △ABC.
• If the cell’s diagonal is “/” (from B to D) the two triangles are △ABD and △BCD. Here the north edge AB belongs to △ABD.

Now, denote by a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ the color (0 or 1) assigned to the triangle in cell (i, j) that touches the north edge. Because the two triangles in a cell must have opposite colors, the triangle on the south edge gets the opposite color, namely 1 – a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎.

──────────────────────────────
Step 3. How the Diagonals Affect Neighbors

Notice that the cell boundaries are shared by adjacent cells. There are two kinds of shared edges:
1. Vertical edges (shared by a cell and the one immediately below it).
2. Horizontal edges (shared by a cell and the one immediately to its right).

(a) Vertical Neighbors:
The south edge of a cell (i, j) is colored 1 – a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎, and the north edge of the cell immediately below (i+1, j) is colored a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎. For these two triangles (which share the vertical edge) to have different colors we must have
  1 – a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ ≠ a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎.
But this inequality is equivalent to
  a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ = a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎.
Thus the vertical condition forces that in any given column the “north–edge color” is the same in every cell.

(b) Horizontal Neighbors:
Now consider two horizontally adjacent cells in the same row. They share the east edge of the left cell and the west edge of the right cell. However, which triangle touches these edges depends on the diagonal:
• In a “\” cell the east edge is touched by the same triangle as the north edge (so its color is a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎).
• In a “/” cell the east edge is touched by the triangle opposite the north–edge one (so its color is 1 – a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎).

Likewise, for the right cell:
• In a “\” cell the west edge is touched by the triangle opposite the north–edge one (color 1 – a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
• In a “/” cell the west edge is touched by the same triangle as the north edge (color a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).

Thus, if we define a function f on a cell by
  f(d, a) = a if the cell’s diagonal is “\” 
  f(d, a) = 1 – a if the cell’s diagonal is “/”,
then the color on the east edge of the left cell is f(d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎, a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎) and the color on the west edge of the right cell is f(d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎, a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎). For these two regions (sharing a horizontal edge) to have different colors we need
  f(d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎, a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎) = f(d₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎, a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎).
In other words, the horizontal condition between the jth and (j+1)th cell in row i is that the “output” of f in the two cells must agree.

A quick check shows that this condition is equivalent to requiring that the number of “switches” (i.e. changes from “\” to “/” or vice‐versa) in that row is even. (To see this, note that if two adjacent cells have the same type then f produces the same value whether you start with a or 1–a; if they have different types then f “flips” the bit, and to end up with the same color as you started you must have an even number of flips.)

──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Counting the “Good” Rows and the Overall Probability

Focus on a fixed row. There are 4 cells so 3 gaps between them. Encode “\” as 0 and “/” as 1. Then the horizontal condition is that the number of indices i = 1, 2, 3 for which the adjacent symbols differ is even. (For example, the row 0,0,0,0 has 0 changes, and the row 0,1,0,1 has 3 changes; only rows with 0 or 2 changes work.)

A short count shows that among the 16 possible 4–term sequences the number with an even number of changes is 8. (For instance, the 2 sequences with no change and the 6 sequences with exactly 2 changes add up to 8.) Thus the probability that a given row satisfies the condition is 8/16 = ½.

Since the rows are independent, the overall probability that every one of the 4 rows has an even number of changes is
  (½)^4 = 1/16.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

Out of the 2^16 possible diagonal assignments, exactly 1/16 yield a configuration in which the 32 triangular regions can be 2–colored (red and blue) so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors. Therefore, the answer is

  1/16.

We will show that if we label each cell’s diagonal by a 0 or 1 (say, letting “0” stand for the “\” diagonal and “1” for the “/” diagonal), then one may prove that the 32 regions produced in the 4×4 board can be 2–colored (with “red” and “blue”) if and only if every 2×2 block of cells has an even number of 1’s. (In other words, if in every 2×2 block the sum mod 2 of the four cell–values is 0.) One may then show that among all 2^(16) possible assignments of 0’s and 1’s to the 16 cells the “good” ones are exactly those 0–1 matrices having the “even‐2×2–block” property and that one may prove in general that an m×n array has exactly 2^(m+n–1) solutions of
  a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ + a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ + a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₊₁₎ = 0 (mod 2)
(with 1 ≤ i ≤ m–1, 1 ≤ j ≤ n–1). (You may check, for example, that a 2×2 board has 2^(2+2–1)=2³=8 solutions out of 16, a 3×3 board has 2^(3+3–1)=2⁵=32 solutions out of 2⁹, etc.)

In our 4×4 case the number of “good” diagonal–configurations is therefore
  2^(4+4–1) = 2⁷ = 128.
Since the total number of configurations is 2^(16) = 65 536, the desired probability is

  128/65 536 = 1/512.

A Brief Explanation of the “2×2–block” Criterion

To explain a little more (without giving every detail):

1. In each cell the drawn diagonal splits the square into two triangular regions. One may check that in every cell one of the two regions touches the top edge and the other touches the bottom edge. (In a “\” cell the top–edge region also touches the right edge, while in a “/” cell it touches the left edge; and vice–versa for the other region.)

2. When two cells share a side the only way for their common boundary segment to be “between” two regions is that in one cell the region touching that side is paired with the appropriate other region. (For example, if a cell on the left has a “\” diagonal then its right–edge region is the one that also touches the top edge; while if it has a “/” then its right–edge region is the one that touches the bottom edge.) One may show that if you try to 2–color all 32 regions (red and blue) so that any two regions sharing an edge get different colors, then a necessary and sufficient condition is that in every 2×2 block the “parity” (i.e. the sum mod 2) of the four cell–values is 0.

3. One may then count (by a short linear–algebra argument over GF(2)) that an m×n array of 0’s and 1’s satisfying
  a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₎ + a₍ᵢ,ⱼ₊₁₎ + a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₎ + a₍ᵢ₊₁,ⱼ₊₁₎ = 0 (mod 2)
has exactly 2^(m+n–1) solutions. (You may verify this in small cases; for a 2×2 board there are 8 solutions, for a 3×3 board 32, etc.)

For a 4×4 board the count is 2^(4+4–1)=2⁷=128 so that the probability is

  128/2^(16) = 128/65 536 = 1/512.

We will show that if one places a diagonal (either “\” or “/”) in each of the 16 unit squares of a 4×4 grid (each choice made independently with probability ½), then a “good” configuration – one for which the 32 resulting triangular regions can be 2–colored (red/blue) so that any two regions sharing an entire edge have opposite colors – occurs with probability 1/512.

In what follows we describe one way to “model” the situation and count the good configurations.

──────────────────────────────
A “Potential‐function” approach

Step 1. Labeling the cells and their triangles

Label the rows 1,…,4 (top to bottom) and the columns 1,…,4 (left to right). In each cell we draw one diagonal. (We imagine the square’s vertices as “top‐left”, “top‐right”, “bottom‐right” and “bottom‐left”.) For convenience we encode the two choices by a 0 or 1:
 • 0 means we draw the “\” (from top–left to bottom–right);
 • 1 means we draw the “/” (from top–right to bottom–left).

Now, observe that the diagonal splits the square into two triangles. One may check that:
 • In a “\” cell (0) one triangle (call it T₀) has its sides along the top and right edges, while the other (T₁) has its sides along the left and bottom edges.
 • In a “/” cell (1) one triangle (again call it T₀) has its sides along the right and bottom edges, while the other (T₁) has its sides along the top and left edges.

In every cell the two triangles share the drawn diagonal (an “internal” edge) so they must receive opposite colors in any proper 2–coloring.

Step 2. How regions in adjacent cells meet

Notice that the boundaries of the cells (the grid lines) remain intact. Thus, regions in neighboring cells may share a common edge. (They never “meet” at a single point only.) In fact, one may check that:
 • Along any vertical edge (say, the right edge of a cell and the left edge of its neighbor to the right) the meeting is always between the T₀ triangle in the left cell and the T₁ triangle in the right cell.
 • Along any horizontal edge (say, the bottom edge of an upper cell and the top edge of the cell immediately below) the “touching” triangles depend on the type of cell. In a “\” cell the triangle touching the bottom is T₁, while in a “/” cell the triangle touching the bottom is T₀. Similarly, in the lower cell a “\” cell has its top edge touched by T₀ and a “/” cell has its top edge touched by T₁.

Thus, if we wish to 2–color the regions (red and blue, say) so that adjacent regions have opposite colors, then in every cell the two triangles must get opposite colors. (This is automatic once we “choose a base color” for one of them.) Moreover, the vertical edges force a further condition. To see this note that along a vertical edge the left cell’s T₀ (whatever its color) meets the right cell’s T₁. Since T₁ is the “opposite” of the base color in its cell, the vertical edge forces the base color in the left cell to equal the base color in the right cell.

It is then natural to “assign a potential” to each cell by declaring that the base color (say, represented by 0 for red and 1 for blue) in a cell is a number c ∈ {0,1} which we will choose so that in that cell T₀ gets color c and T₁ gets the opposite color (1–c). (Once these potentials are chosen the 2–coloring is forced.)

Step 3. The vertical condition forces each row to be constant

Look at two cells in the same row that share a vertical edge. As noted, the vertical edge joins the T₀ of the left cell and the T₁ of the right cell. Since T₁ in the right cell is the opposite of its base color, the edge forces
  c(left cell) = c(right cell).
Thus, in every row the base color must be the same in all 4 cells. (There is no “mixing” within a row.)

So we may describe a configuration by giving, for each row i = 1,…,4, a single number rᵢ ∈ {0,1} which is the base color for every cell in that row.

Step 4. The horizontal condition relates adjacent rows

Now consider a horizontal edge between a cell in row i and the cell immediately below it in row i+1. There are two cases for a given column j:

• If the cell in row i is a “\” (0) then its bottom edge is touched by T₁ (which has color 1–rᵢ). In row i+1, if the cell is “\” (0) then its top edge is touched by T₀ (color rᵢ₊₁); if it is “/” (1) then its top edge is touched by T₁ (color 1–rᵢ₊₁).

• If the cell in row i is “/” (1) then its bottom edge is touched by T₀ (color rᵢ). In row i+1, if the cell is “\” (0) then its top edge is touched by T₀ (color rᵢ₊₁); if it is “/” (1) then its top edge is touched by T₁ (color 1–rᵢ₊₁).

For the two regions meeting along the common horizontal edge to have opposite colors we must have (writing “+” for addition mod 2) an equation that, after a short check, turns out to force the following:

For each column j the “relation” between rᵢ and rᵢ₊₁ is determined by the types in that column. In fact one may show that the condition is equivalent to requiring that for every column j the following holds:
  Either rᵢ = rᵢ₊₁  or  rᵢ = 1–rᵢ₊₁.
But here is the key point: the horizontal edge between the two cells in column j gives a relation that depends on the two cells’ types. However, since the vertical edges forced every row to have a constant base color, the horizontal condition (which must hold for every common edge) implies that for each adjacent pair of rows the “relation” must be the same in every column. In other words, if we write the type (0 or 1) of the cell in row i, column j as xᵢⱼ, then for each adjacent pair of rows (i, i+1) we must have that for every column j the relation
  xᵢⱼ ? xᵢ₊₁ⱼ
is the same. (It cannot happen that in one column the two cells are the same and in another they are different.) One may check that this is equivalent to saying that for each adjacent pair of rows the entire row (as a 4–bit string) is either identical or complementary.

Step 5. Counting the good configurations

Originally each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently (2 choices per cell) so there are 2^(16) total configurations.

Now, thanks to the vertical condition the only “free parameters” are the 4 base–colors r₁, r₂, r₃, r₄ (one per row). However, the horizontal condition forces that for each adjacent pair of rows the second row must equal either the first row or its complement. (For a given row the 4–bit string can be arbitrary; there are 2⁴ = 16 choices. Then for the next row there are exactly 2 choices – be identical to the previous row or be its bitwise complement – and similarly for the next ones.)

Thus the number of “good” row–assignments is
  16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 2³ = 128.
Each such row–assignment corresponds uniquely to a configuration of diagonals that yields a bipartite (2–colorable) arrangement of the 32 triangles.

Therefore the probability that a random configuration is “good” is
  128 / 2^(16) = 128 / 65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The desired probability is 1/512.

An answer in boxed form:
  Probability = 1/512.

So each cell gets one of two possible diagonals, presumably chosen with probability 1/2 each, independent over cells. The drawing of diagonals partitions each square into two triangles. So overall there are 16 cells * 2 = 32 triangular regions. We want the probability that the resulting 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors (i.e. a proper 2-coloring of the regions, i.e. the regions form a bipartite graph with respect to adjacency). The condition is that any two regions that share an edge (i.e. share a common boundary segment, not just a vertex) must have opposite colors. This is like checking if the dual graph of regions is bipartite. But since the regions are triangles, they might share edges in a complicated pattern. But note: The pattern is induced by the diagonals in each cell. We need to compute the probability that the graph of regions (where vertices are regions, and edges are between regions sharing an edge) is bipartite.

We will show that if you choose a diagonal in each of the 16 unit squares (each square’s diagonal being chosen independently with equal chance to be one of the two possibilities), then the 32 resulting triangles can be “two‐colored” (red/blue in such a way that any two regions sharing a full edge have opposite colors) if and only if the following “column‐condition” holds:

  For every pair of horizontally adjacent columns (that is, for columns j and j+1, j = 1,2,3) the “pattern” of diagonal choices is the same in every row. In other words, for each such pair either in every row the cell in column j and the cell in column j+1 have the same diagonal or in every row they have opposite diagonals.

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at this condition and then count the number of “good” configurations.

──────────────────────────────
A “model” for a 2–coloring

Step 1. In each square (cell) draw one of the two diagonals. (We label the two types by 0 and 1. For convenience you may think of 0 as the “\” diagonal and 1 as the “/” diagonal.)

Step 2. In every cell the diagonal splits the square into two triangles. Notice that regardless of which diagonal is drawn the triangle that touches the top edge is always the same (call it the “top‐triangle”) and the other (touching the bottom edge) is its complement. (A short check shows that in a “\” cell the triangle along the right edge is the top–triangle, while in a “/” cell the triangle along the right edge is the other one; similarly for the left edge.)

Step 3. Now suppose we wish to “color” the 32 regions red and blue so that any two regions sharing a full edge get opposite colors. (Regions that meet only at a point need not have different colors.) One way to do this is to “decorate” each cell by choosing a base color for its top–triangle and then declaring that the other triangle gets the opposite color. (That is, if the top–triangle is red then the bottom–triangle is blue and vice‐versa.)

Step 4. Next, look at two cells that share an edge. There are two types of shared edges:
  • A vertical edge (between two cells in the same row).
  • A horizontal edge (between two cells in adjacent rows).

A short check shows that the vertical edges always “work out.” (In fact, the bottom edge of any cell is always opposite in color to its top–triangle; and the top edge of the cell immediately below is just that cell’s top–triangle. Thus if we require that every cell in a given column uses the same base color then the vertical edges are properly “colored.”)

The only potential trouble comes from vertical edges between cells in the same row (i.e. between two horizontally adjacent cells). For example, consider two neighboring cells in the same row. In the left cell the triangle touching the right edge is:
  – the top–triangle if its diagonal is “\” (type 0),
  – the other triangle if its diagonal is “/” (type 1).
In the right cell the triangle touching the left edge is:
  – the other triangle if its diagonal is “\” (type 0),
  – the top–triangle if its diagonal is “/” (type 1).

Thus if we denote by b the base color assigned to a cell then the color on the right edge of a cell is:
  • b if the cell’s diagonal is “\” (0),
  • not b if the cell’s diagonal is “/” (1),
and the color on the left edge of its neighbor is:
  • not b if that neighbor’s diagonal is “\” (0),
  • b if that neighbor’s diagonal is “/” (1).

For the two regions sharing that common vertical edge to have opposite colors we must have

  (color on left edge of right cell) = opposite of (color on right edge of left cell).

A short case–check shows that this forces the following rule: If the two adjacent cells have the same diagonal type then the base colors in the two cells must be equal, and if they have opposite types then the base colors must be opposite.

But here is the key point. Although the base color in a cell is not determined by its diagonal type, the vertical condition (from Step 4) forces that in any fixed column every cell must be given the same base color. (Why? Because any two cells in the same column share a horizontal edge and the condition forces their base colors to be equal.) Thus the only “free” choices are the base colors for the 4 columns (each column gets one color, either red or blue).

Now, look at two horizontally adjacent cells in the same row. Their base colors come from their respective columns. The rule we just derived then tells us that for each row the following must hold:
  • If the left cell’s diagonal is the same as the right cell’s diagonal then the two column–colors must be the same.
  • If the left cell’s diagonal is different from the right cell’s diagonal then the two column–colors must be different.

But the column–colors are global (the same for every row in a given column). Therefore, for a fixed pair of adjacent columns the relation between the diagonals in those two columns must be the same in every row. In other words, for each pair of adjacent columns (columns j and j+1, j = 1,2,3) either in every row the cell in column j and the cell in column j+1 have the same diagonal or in every row they have opposite diagonals.

──────────────────────────────
Counting the “good” configurations

Now, let’s count how many diagonal–configurations yield a 2–colorable picture.

• There are 16 cells. (Each cell independently gets a diagonal, 2 choices per cell, for a total of 2^16 configurations.)

• It is most natural to “group” the cells by columns. In any fixed column the 4 cells can be chosen arbitrarily (2^4 possibilities per column) because no condition relates the choices in different rows in the same column.

• The only restrictions come from the horizontal (adjacent–column) conditions. For each adjacent pair of columns (say, columns j and j+1) the condition is that either
  – for every row i the diagonal in column j equals the diagonal in column j+1, or
  – for every row i the diagonal in column j is the opposite of the diagonal in column j+1.
Given an arbitrary configuration in column j (which can be any 4–tuple of 0’s and 1’s), there are exactly 2 ways to choose the 4–tuple for column j+1 that satisfy the condition (namely, either copy column j exactly or take its complement).

Thus, if we label the columns 1,2,3,4 then:
  – Column 1: 2^4 choices.
  – Column 2: 2 choices (once column 1 is fixed).
  – Column 3: 2 choices (relative to column 2).
  – Column 4: 2 choices (relative to column 3).

So the total number of “good” configurations is
  2^4 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 8 = 128.

Since the total number of configurations is 2^16 = 65,536, the desired probability is

  128 / 65,536 = 1/512.

──────────────────────────────
Final Answer

The probability that the 32 triangular regions can be 2–colored (red and blue with neighboring regions opposite in color) is 1/512.

We will show that if in each cell of a 4×4 grid one chooses (independently and uniformly at random) one of the two possible diagonals, then the 32 triangular regions obtained can be “2‐colored” (red/blue in such a way that any two regions sharing an entire edge have opposite colors) if and only if a certain parity condition holds. In fact, one may prove that a necessary and sufficient condition is that for every “interior vertex” (a point where four cells meet) the sum (mod 2) of certain indicators is 0. (In our setting it turns out that if we encode a cell’s diagonal by a 0–1 variable in a natural way, then the condition is that for every interior vertex the sum of the four surrounding cell–values is 0 mod 2.) One may show that for a 4×4 grid there are 9 such interior vertices but that these 9 linear equations (over GF(2)) are not independent – in fact, one may prove that their rank is 5. (For example, one may check that for a 2×2 grid there is 1 condition and for a 3×3 grid there are 3 independent conditions.) 

To explain a little more:

1. Label the 16 cells by (i,j) with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ 4. In each cell choose a diagonal. (For concreteness you may think of the “\” diagonal as 0 and the “/” diagonal as 1.)  
2. Now, every interior vertex (there are 9 of them in a 4×4 grid) is the meeting point of 4 cells. One may show that if you “travel” once around such a vertex the number of times you are forced to “flip” color (because you cross a cell‐diagonal that has the vertex as an endpoint) is exactly the sum mod 2 of the four cell–values at that vertex. (For example, if the cell in the northwest has a “\” then its diagonal has that vertex as an endpoint; if it has a “/” then it does not. In a similar way the other three cells contribute according to a fixed rule.)  
3. For the cycle around the vertex to be even (so that a 2–coloring is possible locally) the total number of flips must be even. In other words, for every interior vertex the sum of the four surrounding cell–values must be 0 mod 2.

A short linear–algebra exercise shows that among the 9 such equations there are only 5 independent ones. (For instance, one may check by a direct count that in a 2×2 grid there is 1 condition and in a 3×3 grid there are 3.) Consequently, a random assignment of 0’s and 1’s to the 16 cells (each occurring with probability ½) will satisfy these 5 independent conditions with probability

  (½)⁵ = 1/32.

Since the 32 regions can be 2–colored if and only if these conditions hold, the answer to the problem is 1/32.

Thus, the probability that the 32 triangular regions can be colored red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have different colors is

  1/32.

We will show that if in every cell the diagonal is drawn “at random” (each of the two possible diagonals is chosen with probability ½ independently in the 16 cells) then the 32 regions (each cell is cut into 2 triangles) can be “proper‐2–colored” (red and blue so that any two regions sharing an edge have opposite colors) if and only if a certain “global” condition holds. In fact one may prove that a 2–coloring exists if and only if for every pair of cells in adjacent columns the “twist” made by the diagonals is the same in every row. (In other words, if we label the cells by coordinates (i,j) with 1 ≤ i,j ≤ 4 and “mark” the diagonal by a sign ε(i,j) = +1 or –1 according as the diagonal is drawn from the bottom–left to the top–right (“type A”) or from the top–left to the bottom–right (“type B”), then a necessary and sufficient condition for the dual graph of regions to be bipartite is that for each j = 1,2,3 the 4–tuple
  (ε(1,j), ε(2,j), ε(3,j), ε(4,j))
and
  (ε(1,j+1), ε(2,j+1), ε(3,j+1), ε(4,j+1))
are either identical (all +1’s or all –1’s) or are opposites (each entry in the second is the negative of the corresponding entry in the first).)

Below we describe one way to arrive at this answer.

──────────────────────────────
An Outline of One Reasoning

1. Setting up the picture

Label the rows 1,…,4 (top to bottom) and the columns 1,…,4 (left to right). In each cell (i,j) one of the two diagonals is drawn. (Thus there are 2^16 total configurations.) In every cell the diagonal splits the square into two triangles. (For example, if one draws the “main” diagonal from the bottom–left to the top–right then one triangle has the bottom and right sides as part of its boundary while the other has the top and left sides as part of its boundary.) In any event, note that each cell contributes exactly 2 regions and no two regions meet except along a full side (or along the drawn diagonal, which is an interior edge of the cell).

2. How regions meet

Two regions (triangles) that come from two different cells will share a whole edge exactly when the common side of the two cells is “active” in both cells. (For instance, the common vertical edge between the cell in column j and the one in column j+1 is “active” in the left cell if the triangle touching its right side is present and in the right cell if the triangle touching its left side is present.) A short check shows that in every cell the triangle touching the top side is always the same (call it “top”) and the one touching the bottom side is always the same (call it “bottom”). However, which triangle touches the left or right side depends on the diagonal:
 • If the diagonal is drawn from bottom–left to top–right (we call this type A) then the triangle touching the right side is the “bottom” one and the one touching the left side is the “top” one.
 • If the diagonal is drawn from top–left to bottom–right (type B) then the roles are reversed: the triangle touching the right side is the “top” one and the one touching the left side is the “bottom” one.

Thus if we “mark” a cell by a sign ε = +1 when the diagonal is type A and ε = –1 when it is type B, then in every cell the “top” and “bottom” triangles are always present (with the top always coming from the same triangle and the bottom from the other) while the “vertical‐port” (the triangle on the right or left) is given by:
 – In a type A cell (ε = +1): right port = bottom, left port = top.
 – In a type B cell (ε = –1): right port = top, left port = bottom.

3. What does a 2–coloring mean?

We wish to color the 32 regions red and blue so that whenever two regions share a full edge the colors are different. (This is equivalent to saying that the “dual graph” whose vertices are the regions and whose edges connect regions sharing an edge is bipartite.)

A natural idea is to “assign a potential” to each cell. For each cell (i,j) choose a bit p(i,j) ∈ {0,1} and declare that the top triangle gets color p(i,j) and the bottom triangle gets the opposite color, 1 – p(i,j). (You might think of 0 as “red” and 1 as “blue”.) Then one checks that the horizontal edges (which join the top of a cell in one row to the bottom of the cell immediately below) force
  p(i,j) = p(i+1,j)
for every vertical pair of cells in the same column. (There is no choice here; the condition is forced by the fact that the top of the upper cell and the bottom of the lower cell must get opposite colors.)

Now consider a vertical edge between two cells in the same row (say, between cell (i,j) and cell (i,j+1)). The vertical edge joins the right port of the left cell and the left port of the right cell. Using the rules above the color on the right port of cell (i,j) is:
 • 1 – p(i,j) if ε(i,j) = +1,
 • p(i,j)  if ε(i,j) = –1.
Similarly, the color on the left port of cell (i,j+1) is:
 • p(i,j+1)  if ε(i,j+1) = +1,
 • 1 – p(i,j+1) if ε(i,j+1) = –1.
For these two colors to be different we must have (working in ℤ₂):
 – If ε(i,j) and ε(i,j+1) are the same then p(i,j) = p(i,j+1).
 – If they are different then p(i,j) = 1 – p(i,j+1).

But remember that the horizontal condition already forced that in each column all the p–values are equal. (That is, if we write a_j for the common value in column j then p(i,j) = a_j for every row i.) Thus the vertical condition becomes a condition on the 4–vectors of signs in adjacent columns. Namely, for each j = 1,2,3 the 4–tuple in column j and that in column j+1 must be related in the same way in every row; that is, either
  (ε(1,j),…,ε(4,j)) = (ε(1,j+1),…,ε(4,j+1))
or
  (ε(1,j),…,ε(4,j)) = –(ε(1,j+1),…,ε(4,j+1)).
In other words, for each j = 1,2,3 the “relation” between column j and column j+1 must be uniform (the same in every row).

4. Counting the “good” configurations

Now, the ε–values in the 16 cells are chosen independently with probability ½ each so that there are 2^16 total configurations.

Look at the 4 columns. In column 1 the 4–tuple (ε(1,1),…,ε(4,1)) can be arbitrary; there are 2^4 = 16 choices. Then for column 2 the condition is that its 4–tuple must equal either the 4–tuple in column 1 or its negation. That gives 2 choices. Similarly, column 3 has 2 choices (relative to column 2) and column 4 has 2 choices (relative to column 3). Thus the total number of “good” ε–configurations is
  16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 8 = 128.
Since the total number of configurations is 2^16 = 65,536, the desired probability is
  128/65,536 = 1/512.

Step 1. Encoding the Diagonals

In each of the 16 cells we choose a diagonal at random. (There are 2^16 equally likely outcomes.) It is convenient to encode the choice in a cell by a bit:

Now, when two cells share a full side (an edge of the 4×4 square) the following happens. Look at two horizontally adjacent cells. In the left cell the triangle that touches its right side depends on the diagonal:
 • If the left cell is “/” (0) then the triangle along the right edge is the one with vertices top–left, top–right, bottom–right.

 • If the right cell is “/” then the triangle along the left edge is the one with vertices top–left, bottom–left, bottom–right.
 • If the right cell is “\” then the triangle along the left edge is the one with vertices top–left, top–right, bottom–left.

(A similar analysis works for vertical edges between cells in consecutive rows.) For a vertical edge between two adjacent cells the condition is:
 – If the two cells have the same diagonal (both 0 or both 1) then the “flip–choices” in the two cells must be the same.
 – If the two cells have different diagonals then the flip–choices must be opposite.
On the other hand, if you examine a horizontal edge (a common edge between a cell in one row and a cell in the row immediately below) you find that the condition does not depend on the diagonal at all – it forces the “flip–choice” in every cell in a given row to be the same.  • If the two cells’ diagonal bits are equal then the flip–choices must be equal.
 • If the two cells’ diagonal bits are different then the flip–choices must be opposites.

But now observe that in any given row the horizontal edges force all the flip–choices in that row to be identical. (There is no restriction coming from the diagonal choices in this case.) Therefore, if we denote by r₁, r₂, r₃, r₄ the common flip–choice in rows 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively, then the vertical edge conditions tell us that for each pair of consecutive rows the following must hold in every column:
 – Either the two cells in the two rows have the same diagonal bit (in which case we must have rᵢ = rᵢ₊₁),
 – Or they have different diagonal bits (in which case we must have rᵢ + rᵢ₊₁ = 1, i.e. rᵢ and rᵢ₊₁ are opposites).

But note that the flip–choices rᵢ are fixed numbers (0 or 1) for the entire row. Therefore, for a given pair of consecutive rows the condition can be met only if in every column the diagonal bit in the upper cell and the diagonal bit in the lower cell are either always equal or always opposites. In other words, if you write the 4×4 array by rows, then for each adjacent pair of rows the two rows must be either identical or complementary (entry–by–entry).

Step 3. Counting the “Good” Configurations

Since each cell’s diagonal is chosen independently (with 2 choices per cell) there are 2^16 total configurations.

Now, view the 4×4 array as 4 rows of 4 bits each. The only restrictions for a configuration to allow a proper 2–coloring are that for each of the 3 pairs of consecutive rows the two rows are either identical or complementary. (There is no restriction horizontally because, as we saw, the horizontal edges force a common flip in each row but do not relate the diagonal bits.)

• The first row can be any 4–bit string. There are 2^4 = 16 possibilities.
• For the second row, once the first row is given, the only acceptable choices are that the second row equals the first row or equals its complement. That gives 2 choices.
• Similarly, for the third row there are 2 choices (it must equal the second row or be its complement), and for the fourth row there are 2 choices.

Thus the number of “good” configurations is 16 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 × 8 = 128.

Step 4. The Final Probability

The probability that a random configuration of diagonals yields a triangulation whose 32 regions can be 2–colored as required is therefore

  128 / 2^16 = 128 / 65536 = 1/512.

An Alternative (and Quick) Way to See It

Notice that if you view the 4×4 array row–by–row, then the rows are independent and uniformly random. For any fixed row the next row is equally likely to be any of the 16 possible 4–bit strings. The probability that the next row is exactly the same as the given row is 1/16, and the probability that it is the exact complement is also 1/16. Thus the probability that two consecutive rows are either identical or complementary is 2/16 = 1/8. Since there are 3 pairs of consecutive rows (rows 1–2, 2–3, and 3–4) and the rows are chosen independently, the overall probability is

  (1/8)³ = 1/512.

Final Answer

The answer to the problem is 1/512.
